noun:Kugel.tx: From Middle High German kugel(e), of unknown origin. It is not clear whether Middle Dutch coghele, coeghele (modern kogel) is a cognate or rather a borrowing from High German. In the former case it would require a Proto-West Germanic *kugulā. Possibly related with English cudgel, from Proto-West Germanic *kuggil, a derivative of Proto-Germanic *kuggǭ (“cog, swelling”), whence German Kogge …

adj:kaputt.tx: 17th century, from French être capot (“not having won any trick in a card game”, as in German schwarz sein). The further origin is uncertain, though it probably stems from a figurative usage of capot (“hood”); Pfeiffer suggests an image of "a hood pulled over one's head and face" > "restrained and unable to perform actions" (DWDS). Compare Dutch kapot.

noun:Kuh.tx: Inherited from Middle High German kuo, from Old High German kuo, from Proto-West Germanic *kō, from Proto-Germanic *kōz, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷṓws.

noun:Käfer.tx: From Middle High German këvere, from Old High German chëvar, chëviro, from Proto-West Germanic *kefrō. Akin to English chafer, Dutch kever.

adj:kalt.tx: From Middle High German and Old High German kalt, from Proto-West Germanic *kald. Cognates Cognate to Low German kold, koolt, Dutch koud, English cold, Danish kold, Swedish kall.

adv:kalt.tx: From Middle High German and Old High German kalt, from Proto-West Germanic *kald. Cognates Cognate to Low German kold, koolt, Dutch koud, English cold, Danish kold, Swedish kall.

noun:Kutsche.tx: Borrowed from Hungarian kocsi, from the village of Kocs. Doublet of Coach.

noun:Krümel.tx: Old diminutive of Krume, which is now less common in the simplex form. An originally Central and Low German word that has widely replaced the Upper German Brosame in standard usage. From Middle High German (Central German) krume, reinforced by cognate Middle Low German krume, krōme. From Proto-Germanic *krumô, *krūmô (“fragment, crumb”). Cognate with English crumb. Also related to Dutch kruim, …

noun:Käse.tx: Inherited from Middle High German kæse, from Old High German kāsi, from Proto-West Germanic *kāsī (“cheese”).

verb:kleben.tx: From Middle High German kleben, from Old High German klebēn (“to stick”), from Proto-West Germanic *klibēn.

adj:keck.tx: From Middle High German këc, Upper German form of quëc, from Old High German quëc, from Proto-West Germanic *kwiku, from Proto-Germanic *kwikwaz, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃wós (“alive”). The Central German form survives in Quecksilber and erquicken. From Low German stems the doublet quick (chiefly in quicklebendig). Cognate with Dutch kwiek, English quick; further with Latin vīvus, Russian живой (živoj).

noun:Kraut.tx: Inherited from Middle High German krūt, from Old High German krūt, chrūt, from Proto-West Germanic *krūd (“plant, vegetable, herb”).

noun:Krieg.tx: From Middle High German kriec, from Old High German krig, from Proto-West Germanic *krīg. Cognate with Bavarian Kriag, Alemannic German Chrieg.

noun:Kehle.tx: From Middle High German kële, from Old High German kela, from Proto-West Germanic *kelā, from Proto-Germanic *kelǭ. Cognate with English jowl (“loose flesh around the cheeks and lower jaw”).

noun:Küche.tx: From Middle High German küche, from Old High German chuhhina, from late Proto-West Germanic *kukinā, from Late Latin cocīna, from earlier coquīna.

noun:Kessel.tx: From Middle High German keȥȥel, from Old High German keȥȥil, from Proto-West Germanic *katil (“kettle”).

verb:klettern.tx: An iterative formed from Early New High German kletten, from Proto-Indo-European *gleyt- (“to cling to, cleave, stick”), from *gley- (“to stick, smear”). Related to Klette (“burr”) and Kleid (“dress”) (DWDS). Cognate with Hunsrik klettre.

verb:kämmen.tx: From Middle High German kemmen, kemben, from Old High German kemben, from Proto-Germanic *kambijaną (“to comb”).

verb:keimen.tx: From Middle High German kīmen, from kīm, kīme (“sprout”) (see Keim). Supplanted or merged with Middle High German kīnen (“to sprout”), from Old High German kīnan, from Proto-Germanic *kīnaną (“to germinate; sprout”).

verb:kommen.tx: From Middle High German quëmen, komen, kumen, from Old High German quëman (rarer cuman, chuman), from Proto-West Germanic *kweman, from Proto-Germanic *kwemaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷem-. Cognate with Low German kamen, Dutch komen, English come, Danish komme.

adj:klein.tx: Inherited from Middle High German klein, kleine, from Old High German kleini, from Proto-West Germanic *klainī (“shining, fine, splendid, tender”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *gleh₁y- (“to cleave, stick”). Cognate with Dutch klein and English clean. Doublet of clean. For a similar semantic development, cf. zierlich (orig. "decorative", today "petite").

adj:kurz.tx: From Middle High German kurz, from Old High German kurz, from Proto-West Germanic *kurt, from Latin curtus. Compare also native Old High German *skurz, scurz and Middle High German schurz. Cognate with Dutch and Low German kort, English curt, Swedish kort.

adv:kurz.tx: From Middle High German kurz, from Old High German kurz, from Proto-West Germanic *kurt, from Latin curtus. Compare also native Old High German *skurz, scurz and Middle High German schurz. Cognate with Dutch and Low German kort, English curt, Swedish kort.

noun:Kopf.tx: From Middle High German kopf (“drinking vessel”), from Old High German kopf, chopf, kupf (“mug, bowl, head”), from Proto-West Germanic *kopp, from Proto-Germanic *kuppaz (“round object, bowl, crown of the head”), from Proto-Indo-European *gew- (“to turn, bend, arch, curve”). Cognate with German Low German Kopp (“head”), Dutch kop (“head”), Saterland Frisian Kop (“head”), Yiddish קאָפּ (kop, …

noun:Kummer.tx: From Middle High German kumber (“debris, rubble, obstruction, distress, encumbrance, confiscation”). Cognate with Luxembourgish Kommer, Dutch kommer, Old Frisian kummer. * Probably from Old French *combre (“obstruction, barrier”), combrer (“to hinder”), from Medieval Latin combrus (“barricade”), usually said to be from either Latin cumulus (“heap”) or Gaulish *komberū << Proto-Celtic *kombereti …

noun:Katze.tx: Inherited from Middle High German katze, Old High German kazza, from Proto-West Germanic *kattā. Akin to Old English catt (“cat”).

noun:Krone.tx: From Middle High German krōne, from Old High German krōna, corōna, from Proto-West Germanic *korōnā (“crown”).

noun:Kaffee.tx: From French café, from Italian caffè, from Ottoman Turkish قهوه (kahve), from Arabic قَهْوة (qahwa). First attested in the 17th century. The variants with -o-, which fell into disuse around 1800, are from Dutch koffie and English coffee. Doublet of Café.

noun:Kai.tx: 17th century, from Dutch kaai, from Middle Dutch kaey (whence also through hypercorrection Dutch kade). The word is ultimately Celtic, but it is unsettled whether the Dutch form is borrowed via Old French kay, as traditionally held, or indeed vice versa.

noun:Kaiser.tx: Inherited from Middle High German keiser, from Old High German keisar, keisur, from Proto-West Germanic *kaisar (“emperor”), from Proto-Germanic *kaisaraz, borrowed from Latin Caesar. Doublet of Cäsar and Zar.

noun:Kakao.tx: Borrowed from Spanish cacao, from Classical Nahuatl cacahuatl (“cacao bean”).

noun:Kalium.tx: Coined by Ludwig Wilhelm Gilbert in 1809 from German Kali, as a replacement for the earlier term English potassium.

noun:Kamera.tx: Borrowed from New Latin camera obscūra (“dark chamber”), from Latin camera (“chamber, bedchamber”). Doublet of Kammer and Kamurke.

noun:Kappa.tx: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek κάππα (káppa).

noun:Karaoke.tx: From Japanese カラオケ (karaoke), from 空 (kara, “empty”) + オケ (oke, “orchestra”), the latter being an abbreviation of オーケストラ (ōkesutora), from English orchestra. The German word may also have been borrowed in part through English karaoke.

noun:Kater.tx: From Middle High German katere, from Old High German kataro, from Proto-West Germanic *kataʀō (“male cat; tomcat”), akin to Yiddish קאָטער (koter), German Low German Kater, Dutch kater, Saterland Frisian Koater, English caterwaul, Luxembourgish Kueder.

noun:Katzenjammer.tx: Katze (“cat”) + -n- + Jammer (“wailing; lamentation”). According to one source, the “hangover” sense derives from earlier Kotzen-Jammer (literally “puke-misery”).

noun:Kelvin.tx: Named after Irish-born Scottish physicist William Thomson, Lord Kelvin. For the surname see Kelvin.

noun:Kern.tx: From Middle High German kërne, kërn, from Old High German kërno, from Proto-Germanic *kernô (“core, kernel”).

noun:Khan.tx: From Old French chan, from Medieval Latin canus, caanus, of Turkic origin, from Old Turkic xān (“Central Asian khan”), probably ultimately of non-Turkic (Central Asian) origin.

noun:Kies.tx: From Middle High German kis. Either the basic form of, or a backformation from Old High German kisil, from Proto-West Germanic *kesul, whence Kiesel. See there for more.

noun:Kind.tx: From Middle High German kint, from Old High German kind, from Proto-West Germanic *kind, from Proto-Germanic *kindą, *kinþą, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁- (“to give birth”).

noun:Kiosk.tx: Borrowed from French kiosque, from Italian chiosco, from Ottoman Turkish كوشك (köşk), from Persian کوشک (kôšk). Compare also modern Turkish köşk (“pavillion”).

noun:Kitsch.tx: From the dialectal imitative verb kitschen (“to smear”).

noun:Knacker.tx: knacken + -er. Meaning "geezer" possibly related to Yiddish אַלטער קאַקער (alter kaker).

noun:Knochen.tx: From Middle High German knoche, from Old High German knohha, from Proto-West Germanic *knokō (“bone, joint”). Displaced earlier Bein for "bone" in most contexts. Compare Dutch knook (“bone”), knokkel (“knuckle”), knekel (“bone (of a dead person)”), English knuckle, Danish kno and Swedish knoge (both “knuckle”).

noun:Kobra.tx: From Portuguese cobra, from Latin colubra.

noun:Koffer.tx: From Late Middle High German koffer, from Middle Dutch coffer, from Old French cofre.

noun:Kolonie.tx: 16th century, borrowed from Latin colōnia, in part through Middle French colonie. Doublet of Köln.

noun:Kondom.tx: 19th century borrowing from English condom, further etymology uncertain.

noun:Kot.tx: From Middle High German quāt, from Old High German quāt, from Proto-West Germanic *kwād.

noun:Kritik.tx: Borrowed from French critique, itself from Latin criticus, from Ancient Greek κριτικός (kritikós). Attested since the 17th century.

noun:Känguru.tx: 18th century, from English kangooroo, from Guugu Yimidhirr gangurru (“eastern grey kangaroo”).

noun:Kate.tx: 19th century, from Low German Kaat, Kate, from Middle Low German kāte, a late spelling of kōte, from Old Saxon *kota, from Proto-West Germanic *kotā, from Proto-Germanic *kutǭ ~ *kutą (“stall, tent”), whence also Dutch kot, English cot, cottage. The a-spelling reflects the merger of â, ā, ō into /ɔː/ in most Low German dialects; Standard German /aː/ is analogous. The spelling Kote may have been …

noun:Kollegium.tx: Borrowed from Latin collēgium. Doublet of Kolleg and College.

noun:Kichererbse.tx: From Kicher (“chickpea”), from Middle High German kicher, from Old High German kihhira, + Erbse (“pea”).

noun:Klaue.tx: From Middle High German klāwe, from Old High German klāwa, from Proto-Germanic *klēwō. Immediately cognate with Luxembourgish Klo, Westphalian Low German Klao(we), West Frisian klei, and possibly Dutch klauw. Also related with English claw (from Proto-Germanic *klawō) and Danish klo (from *klōwō).

noun:Knoblauch.tx: From Early New High German Knobloch, from Middle High German knobelouch, with dissimilation from klobelouch from Old High German chlobalouh (literally “clove-leek”), from Proto-West Germanic *klobulauk; from now dialectal klieben (“to cleave”) and Lauch (“leek”). The dissimilated kl- was adapted to the large group of terms for thick objects beginning with kn- (cf. Knopf, Knoten, Knolle, etc.). …

noun:Keil.tx: From Middle High German kīl, from Old High German kīl, from earlier *kīdla-, from the same root as Proto-West Germanic *kīnan (“to split; crack”). Cognate with Vilamovian kajł.

noun:Kuchen.tx: From Middle High German kuoche, from Old High German kuohho, from Proto-Germanic *kōkô. Compare Dutch koek. Doublet of Quiche.

noun:Keks.tx: Borrowed from English cakes, 1900s. Popularized by German food company Bahlsen which changed the brand name of their biscuits from Leibniz-Cakes to Leibniz-Keks in 1911; at the time, the plural was also Keks. Compare Danish kiks, Estonian keeks, Faroese keks, Finnish keksi, Icelandic kex, Norwegian kjeks, and Swedish kex, all ‘cookie, biscuit, cracker’.

noun:Kacke.tx: An onomatopoeic creation relating to the sound a baby makes when pressing while defecating (“a-a-”); compare Aa machen as well as Latin cacō, Ancient Greek κακκάω (kakkáō).

noun:Kupfer.tx: From Middle High German kupfer, from Old High German kupfar, from Proto-West Germanic *kopr (“copper”).

noun:Kackwurst.tx: Compound of Kacke (“caca, crap”) or kacken (“to crap, to shit”) + Wurst (“sausage”). From the similarity of feces with sausage (in form).

noun:Kümmel.tx: From Middle High German kümel, kumel, from Old High German kumil, from Proto-West Germanic *kumil (“caraway, cumin (seed)”).

noun:Kreuz.tx: From Middle High German kriuze, from Old High German kruzi, from Latin crux (gen. crucis).

noun:Kotflügel.tx: Probably because one of its functions at invention time was to keep feces (Kot) from the street away from the passengers of the first, quite open cars.

noun:Kaviar.tx: Borrowed from Venetan caviaro, ultimately from Classical Persian خَاوْیَار (xāwyār). See English caviar for more.

noun:Kartoffel.tx: From older Tartuffel or Tartüffel (18th c.), from Italian tartufolo, diminutive of tartufo (“truffle”), from Medieval Latin *territūberum or Latin terrae tūber (“tuber of the earth”). The use as an ethnic nickname is due to the prominence of potatoes in German cuisine. Compare Spaghetti (“Italian”), Käskopp (“Dutch person”).

noun:Kümmelblättchen.tx: From Kümmel (“caraway”) + Blättchen (“little card”). The first element is actually a folk etymology, and is an alteration of Hebrew גִּימֶל (gímel, “the third letter of the Hebrew alphabet”).

noun:Käfig.tx: From Middle High German kevje, from Old High German chevia, from Latin cavea (“cage”).

noun:Kalb.tx: From Middle High German kalp, from Old High German kalb, from Proto-West Germanic *kalb, from Proto-Germanic *kalbaz, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷolbʰo- (“womb, animal young”). Compare Dutch kalf, English calf, Danish kalv.

noun:Kindergarten.tx: Kind (“child”) + -er- + Garten (“garden”). Coined by German pedagogue Friedrich Fröbel in 1840 in the metaphorical sense of "place where children can grow in a natural way", not in the literal sense of "garden".

noun:Kerze.tx: From Middle High German kerze, from Old High German kerza, charza, from either Latin cērāta (“covered with wax”) or Latin charta (“sheet of papyrus”, in this case referring to layers of birch bark from which candles were made). The latter explanation is typically preferred, though the former is semantically more suggestive. Compare Dutch kaars, Hunsrik Kerz, Luxembourgish Käerz.

adj:klar.tx: From Middle High German klār, clār, formally from Middle Low German klār or Middle Dutch claer and reinforced by Old French cler, both from Latin clārus (“bright”). Doublet of klaro.

adv:klar.tx: From Middle High German klār, clār, formally from Middle Low German klār or Middle Dutch claer and reinforced by Old French cler, both from Latin clārus (“bright”). Doublet of klaro.

intj:klar.tx: From Middle High German klār, clār, formally from Middle Low German klār or Middle Dutch claer and reinforced by Old French cler, both from Latin clārus (“bright”). Doublet of klaro.

noun:Kitzler.tx: From kitzeln (“to tickle”) + -er. In the “clitoris” sense, likely a calque of Ancient Greek κλειτορίς (kleitorís), based on a folk etymology deriving it from the verb κλειτοριάζω (kleitoriázō, “touch or titillate lasciviously, tickle”).

noun:Klitoris.tx: From post-Classical Latin clītoris, from Koine Greek κλειτορίς (kleitorís); see English clitoris.

noun:Kirche.tx: From Middle High German kirche, from Old High German kirihha, from Proto-West Germanic *kirikā.

noun:Knie.tx: From Middle High German knie, from Old High German kneo, from Proto-West Germanic *kneu, from Proto-Germanic *knewą (compare Dutch knie, Low German Knee, Knie, English knee, Danish knæ, Swedish knä), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵnéwo-, a thematic derivative of Proto-Indo-European *ǵónu. Compare Hittite 𒄀𒉡 (genu), Latin genū, Tocharian A kanweṃ (dual), Tocharian B kenī, Ancient Greek γόνυ (gónu, …

verb:kotzen.tx: From an earlier koptzen, from Middle High German koppezen, intensive form of koppen (“to spit”), likely of onomatopoeic origin.

noun:Koralle.tx: From Middle High German koral, from Old French coral, from Latin corallium.

noun:Küken.tx: Via German Low German from Middle Low German kuken, from Old Saxon *kiukīn, from Proto-West Germanic *kiukīn (“chicken”). Cognate with Dutch kuiken, English chicken. A related form is Middle High German kuchil, whence now obsolete Küchlein.

noun:Kerbtier.tx: From Kerbe + Tier, coined by Joachim Heinrich Campe in 1791 to replace the Latinate term Insekt.

noun:Kerbe.tx: From Middle High German kërbe (“incision, notch”), from Old High German *kerba, from Proto-West Germanic *kerbā, from Proto-Germanic *kerbǭ, related to *kerbaną (“to cut, carve”). Cognate with German Low German Karve, Middle Dutch kerve, Saterland Frisian Käärwe, Old Norse kjarf (“bundle”), Old English cyrf (“incision”) (whence English kerf).

noun:Kunst.tx: From Middle High German and Old High German kunst (“knowledge”), first attested in c. 9th century; related to the verb können. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *kunstiz (“knowledge, ability”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃- (“to know”). Cognate with Dutch kunst, West Frisian keunst, Swedish konst.

noun:Künstler.tx: From Kunst (“art”) + -ler; cognate with Hunsrik Kinstler, Luxembourgish Kënschtler.

noun:Knackwurst.tx: From the sound when the sausage cracks. Equivalent to Knack + Wurst.

verb:knacken.tx: From Middle High German knacken, probably ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *knokōn (“to knock”). Related to Middle Low German knaken, knakken, knacken, German Low German knacken. Compare also Middle Low German knicken (“to bend, snap”).

noun:Kommunismus.tx: Coined by German-born philosopher Karl Marx and German philosopher, sociologist and economist Friedrich Engels in 1848 in the Manifest der Kommunistischen Partei (“Manifesto of the Communist Party”), from French communisme (coined in 1840), formed from commun (“common”), from Latin commūnis, and the suffix -isme (“-ism”).

noun:Köcher.tx: From Middle High German köcher, itself with analogical umlaut from older kochære, from Old High German kohhāri, itself by adaptation to the suffix -āri from older kohhar, from Proto-West Germanic *kokar, said to be from Hunnic *kukur, perhaps ultimately from Proto-Mongolic *kökexür.

noun:Kammer.tx: From Middle High German kamer, from Old High German kamara, from Proto-West Germanic *kamarā (“chamber”). Doublet of Kamera (“camera”) and Kamurke (“chamber”).

noun:Kamel.tx: Inherited from Middle High German kemel, kemmel, kembel, borrowed during the Crusades from Medieval Greek κάμηλος (kámēlos), probably in part also from Arabic جَمَل (jamal), which best explains the e-vocalism (as Arabic a is [æ] or even [ɛ] in this word). The modern form with final stress is a 16th-century learned alteration after Latin camēlus, itself from Ancient Greek, from a Semitic language. …

noun:Kamelie.tx: It was named after Moravian Jesuit missionary, pharmacist and naturalist Joseph Kamel (‘Camellus’) (1661–1706). The Czech surname Kamel is a variant of Kamil, who gave a description of the plants of East Asia.

noun:Kanzler.tx: From Middle High German kanzelære, from Old High German canzilāri (ca. 900), borrowed from Late Latin cancellārius, derived from Latin cancellus. By surface analysis, Kanzel + -er, but semantically pertaining more closely to Kanzlei (itself derived from the former). Compare English chancellor. The use for a head of government developed in a monarchic context from that for a senior administrator. …

verb:krepieren.tx: Borrowed from Italian crepare, first only as slang among soldiers in the context of the Thirty Years' War. Since the 17th century.

noun:Krabbe.tx: Borrowed from Low German and Middle Low German krabbe. Cognate with Dutch krab, English crab, Old Norse krabbi (Norwegian krabbe, Swedish krabba). Ultimately from the same root as krabbeln. See crab for more.

noun:Kappe.tx: From Middle High German kappe, from Old High German kappa, kapha, from Proto-West Germanic *kappā (“coat, hood”). Doublet of Kapuze and Cappuccino.

noun:Knorpel.tx: From Middle High German knorpel- (“cartilage.”). Cognate with Hunsrik Knorvel, Dutch knobbel, Low German knusperknaken (“cartilaginous bone”).

noun:Kröte.tx: From Middle High German krotte, kröte, krëte, from Old High German chrota, krota, kreta (“toad”), from Proto-West Germanic *krodu.

noun:Keim.tx: From Middle High German kīm, kīme, from Old High German kīmo, distantly related to English chink.

noun:Klecks.tx: A German Low German [Term?] and Central German derivative in -s from the now archaic verb klecken (“to splash”).

noun:Kohle.tx: From Middle High German kole f alongside commoner kol n, from Old High German kol n, from Proto-West Germanic *kol. The feminine form is chiefly of Central and Low German origin (Middle Low German kōle f). Cognate with Dutch kool f, Danish kul n, English coal.

noun:Kapuze.tx: Late 15th century, borrowed from Italian cappuccio (“hood, cowl”). Compare earlier Middle High German kabütze from Medieval Latin caputium. Doublet of Kappe, Kapuziner, and Cappuccino.

noun:Kasten.tx: From Middle High German kaste, from Old High German kasto, from Proto-West Germanic *kastō.

noun:Kaste.tx: From Portuguese or Spanish casta (“lineage, breed, race”), of uncertain origin.

noun:Klette.tx: From Middle High German klette, from Old High German kletta f, kletto m, from Proto-Germanic *klīþô, from Proto-Indo-European *gleyt- (“to cling to, cleave, stick”), from *gley- (“to stick, smear”). Cognate with Old Saxon kledda f, kleddo m and Middle Low German klette. Related to klettern (“to climb”) and Kleid (“dress”), also Middle Dutch clisse, Dutch klis, Old English cliþe, clāte and English …

noun:König.tx: From Middle High German künec, from Old High German kuning (rarer kunig), from Proto-West Germanic *kuning, from Proto-Germanic *kuningaz. The development Old High German -ning → later -nig is regular (see Pfennig). The modern vocalism -ö- is chiefly Central and Low German; compare Middle Low German köninc, from Old Saxon kuning. Cognate with Old Dutch kuning (whence Dutch koning), Old English …

noun:Koordination.tx: Learned borrowing from Late Latin coōrdinātio, 19th century.

adj:knorke.tx: Unclear; possibly originated as a rhyme for Lorke (“watery coffee”), as a derivation from knorrig (“knotty, gnarled; rough, coarse; sturdy, robust”) (compare Middle High German knorre, English knar, Old Norse knǫrr, and for the semantic develoment English gnarly) using the Low German diminutive suffix -ke, or from the play Die Familie Knorke by Rudolf Melzer.

noun:Kirsche.tx: From Middle High German kirse, from Old High German kirsa, from Proto-West Germanic *kirsijā, from Late Latin ceresia.

verb:können.tx: From Middle High German künnen, kunnen, from Old High German kunnan, from Proto-West Germanic *kunnan, from Proto-Germanic *kunnaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃- (“to know”). The umlauted ö in the infinitive and plural present—as well as the umlaut in the other modal verbs mögen (“to like”), müssen (“to have to”), and dürfen (“to be allowed to”)—is unexpected from an historical point of view. …

verb:kloppen.tx: Central and Low German form (and doublet) of klopfen (“to knock”). The verb was adopted into standard German, in its rougher sense, via the modern vernaculars. An older standard word is the derivative Klöppel (“clapper”). Compare klappen. Cognate with Dutch kloppen.

verb:kosten.tx: From Middle High German kosten, from Old French coster, from Latin cōnstō.

verb:kennen.tx: From Middle High German kennen, from Old High German kennen, from Proto-West Germanic *kannijan (“to know”), from Proto-Germanic *kannijaną (“to know”), a causative form of *kunnaną formed with the suffix *-janą. Cognate to Bavarian kennan, Dutch and Low German kennen, Scots and English ken (“to know”), Yiddish קענען (kenen).

pron:kein.tx: From Middle High German kein, back-formation of original nekein (“not any”), from Old High German nihein, from Proto-West Germanic *nehwain, from Proto-Germanic *nehw ainaz (“not any”). Compare Dutch geen, Yiddish קיין (keyn). More at none.

adj:klasse.tx: Adjectival form of Klasse (“class, grouping; class, excellence”).

noun:Kuss.tx: From Middle High German kus, kos, from Old High German kus, kos, from Proto-West Germanic *koss. Compare Dutch kus, English kiss, Danish kys.

noun:Konsonant.tx: Borrowed from Latin (littera) cōnsonāns (“consonant”) (accusative singular cōnsonantem).

noun:Kampf.tx: From Middle High German kampf, from Old High German kampf, from Proto-West Germanic *kamp (“field, battlefield”). The word originally referred to the “battlefield”, but early on developed the sense “battle, fight” in High German.

verb:küssen.tx: From Middle High German küssen, from Old High German kussen, from Proto-West Germanic *kussijan. Compare Dutch kussen, English kiss, Danish kysse.

noun:Kreide.tx: From Middle High German krīde, from Old High German krīda, from Proto-West Germanic *krīdā.

noun:Kohl.tx: From Middle High German kōl, from Old High German kōl, kōlo, kōli, ultimately from Latin caulis.

noun:Korb.tx: From Middle High German korp, from Old High German korb, chorp, from Proto-West Germanic *korb. The sense “rejection of a (romantic) request” is formed back from the expressions einen Korb geben (“to so reject”), einen Korb kriegen (“to be so rejected”). These derive from certain older customs, which involved a bottomless basket as a symbol of the end or inexistence of love. The further origin of …

noun:Kino.tx: Clipping of Kinematograph m. Originally also used a masculine noun (der Kino).

verb:kochen.tx: From Middle High German kochen, from Old High German kohhōn, from Proto-West Germanic *kokōn (“to cook”).

noun:Kloß.tx: From Middle High German klōz, from Old High German klōz, from Proto-Germanic *klautaz, ablaut form of Proto-Germanic *klūtaz, from Proto-Indo-European *glūdos. Related to Middle Low German klōt, Dutch kloot, Old Norse klútr (“kerchief”) (whence Danish klud), English clout, dialectal Russian глуда (gluda). Doublet of Cloud. More at English cleat.

noun:Klotz.tx: From Middle High German kloz (“stump; ball”), from Old High German kloz (“stump; ball”), from Proto-West Germanic *klott; related to German Kloß (“lump”).

verb:kaufen.tx: From Middle High German koufen, from Old High German koufōn, from Proto-West Germanic *kaupōn. Cognate with Bavarian kaufn, Alemannic German chauffe, Dutch kopen, Old English ċēapian, English cheap.

noun:Kauf.tx: From Middle High German kouf, from Old High German kouf (“trade, barter, commerce”), from Proto-West Germanic *kaup. Cognates Related to Ancient Greek κάπηλος (kápēlos, “huckster”), English cheap, North Frisian kuup (“purchase”), West Frisian keap (“purchase, buy, acquisition”), Dutch koop (“buy, purchase, deal”), kopen (“to buy, purchase, shop”), Low German kopen (“to buy”), Swedish köp …

noun:Koch.tx: From Middle High German koch, from Old High German choch, from Proto-West Germanic *kok (“a cook”).

phrase:Kyrie eleison.tx: Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin Kȳrie eleison, borrowed from Ancient Greek Κῡ́ριε ἐλέησον (Kū́rie eléēson, “Lord, have mercy”).

verb:klären.tx: From Middle High German klæren; from klar.

adj:krank.tx: From Middle High German krank, from Old High German *krank, from Proto-West Germanic *krank, from Proto-Germanic *krangaz, *krankaz (“crooked, weak”). Cognate with English crank and archaic Dutch krank.

noun:Knödel.tx: From Upper German dialects, from Middle High German knödel (“dumpling, noodle”), equivalent to Knoten + -el. Cognate to Yiddish קניידל (kneydl), Bavarian Knedl, Dutch knoedel, Middle Low German knudel, knūdel, German Low German Knudel (“lump, mass”).

adv:kaum.tx: From Middle High German kūme, from Old High German kūmo, from Proto-Germanic *kūmaz, *kūmijaz (“weak, pitiful, frail”), from Proto-Indo-European *gewH- (“to call, cry”). Cognate with English comely and archaic Dutch kuim (“barely”).

noun:Kellner.tx: From Middle High German kelnære, from Old High German kelnere, from Medieval Latin cellenarius (“(wine) cellar administrator”), from Late Latin cellārium (“pantry”), with influence of Keller, itself ultimately from the same Latin source.

verb:kreuzen.tx: From Middle High German kriuzen (“to mark with a cross; crucify”), alteration (after the noun kriuze) of older krūzen, from Old High German krūzōn (“to crucify”). Equivalent to Kreuz + -en. The sense “cruise, patrol” (17th c.) is a semantic loan from Dutch kruisen, whence also English cruise.

noun:Knopf.tx: From Middle High German knopf, from Old High German knopf, from Proto-Germanic *knuppaz (“lump, clod”). Cognate with Hunsrik Knopp, Luxembourgish Knapp, Dutch knoop.

noun:Kelch.tx: From Middle High German kelich, from Old High German kelih, from Proto-West Germanic *kalik (“chalice”).

noun:Kastanie.tx: From Middle High German kastānie, corrupted by Old French chastaigne, from Old High German kestina, kestinna, from Proto-West Germanic *kastannjā (“chestnut”).

noun:Kost.tx: From Middle High German kost(e), from Old High German kosta, deverbal from kostōn (“to try, to taste”).

noun:Klinke.tx: A Low and Central German word, from Middle Low German and northern Middle High German klinke (“latch”), from Proto-West Germanic *klinku (“latch”). Eventually derived from Proto-Germanic *klinganą, probably through the sense “to cling”, alternatively through the sense “to sound” (English clink, German klingen, compare also Klinge (“blade”)). Cognate with Dutch klink, French clenche.

adj:knapp.tx: From Middle Low German knap, probably related to Old Norse hneppr (“button”) and hneppa (“pinch”), all from Proto-Germanic *knappô, *knappa-, which is perhaps related to Proto-West Germanic *knappō (“knob, boy”) or Proto-Germanic *knuppaz (“lump, clod”), though the semantic gaps are non-trivial. Cognate with Dutch knap, but of uncertain ultimate origin. Also compare Danish næppe (“hardly at all”).

adv:knapp.tx: From Middle Low German knap, probably related to Old Norse hneppr (“button”) and hneppa (“pinch”), all from Proto-Germanic *knappô, *knappa-, which is perhaps related to Proto-West Germanic *knappō (“knob, boy”) or Proto-Germanic *knuppaz (“lump, clod”), though the semantic gaps are non-trivial. Cognate with Dutch knap, but of uncertain ultimate origin. Also compare Danish næppe (“hardly at all”).

noun:Kleid.tx: From Middle High German kleit, from Old High German *kleid, from Proto-Germanic *klaiþą, from Proto-Indo-European *gleyt-. Cognate with Dutch kleed, Low German Kleid, English cloth. Possibly related to klettern, Klette, Klei.

noun:Kauz.tx: Inherited from Middle High German kūz, kūze, from Old High German *kūz, from Proto-West Germanic *kūt, from Proto-West Germanic *kūt (“bird of prey”), from Proto-Indo-European *gū- (“to cry, screech”). Cognate with Old English cȳta (“kite, bittern”). See kite. For the sense "crank, old codger" compare English coot (“a foolish or eccentric old person”), which also refers to the bird known as the coot.

noun:Kabeljau.tx: Circa 1600, from Middle Low German kabbelouw (14th c.), from Middle Dutch cabbeliau, cabelliau (12th c.), from Old Dutch cabillau, possibly from Latin baculum (“stick, staff”), referring to the way cod were split and dried on wooden sticks. Or, with metathesis from/influenced by Basque bakailao (“cod”), Portuguese bacalhau (“cod”). The contemporary form was probably reinforced by modern Dutch …

noun:Kachel.tx: From Middle High German kachel, kachele, from Old High German chachala, from Vulgar Latin *cacculus, from cāccabus (“cooking pot”), from Ancient Greek κάκκαβος (kákkabos, “a pot or a pan”). Cognate with Alemannic German Kakel.

noun:Kälte.tx: From Middle High German kelte, from Old High German kaltī, from Proto-West Germanic *kaldī. Analysable as kalt + -e. Cognate with Dutch kou, koude, an alteration of Middle Dutch kelde (similarly perhaps English cold).

noun:Kahn.tx: An originally only Central and Low German word, spread by Luther. From northern Middle High German kane and Middle Low German kāne, from Old High German and Old Saxon *kano, all from Proto-West Germanic *kanō, from Proto-Germanic *kanô (“vessel, boat”).

noun:Kalk.tx: From Middle High German kalc, from Old High German kalk, from Proto-West Germanic *kalk.

noun:Kamm.tx: From Middle High German kamb, camb, chamb, from Old High German chamb, from Proto-West Germanic *kamb, from Proto-Germanic *kambaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵómbʰos (“tooth”).

noun:Kante.tx: Via Middle Low German kant, kante from Middle Dutch kant, itself from Latin canthus (“tire, edge of a wheel”), from Gaulish *cantos, from Proto-Celtic *kantos (“corner, rim”). The Latin spelling is influenced by Ancient Greek κανθός (kanthós, “corner of the eye, tire, etc.”).

verb:kauen.tx: From Middle High German kūwen, kiuwen, kewen, from Old High German kūwen, kiuwan, from Proto-West Germanic *keuwan. Cognate with Dutch kauwen, Low German käwwen, West Frisian koaie, kôgje, English chew. The form shows the Central German development of Middle High German -iuw- → -ūw-, which is only sporadically reflected in the modern standard language (compare brauen). The expected form can still …

noun:Kegel.tx: From Middle High German kegel, from Old High German chegil, kegil (“peg”), especially pegs for a tent (zeltchegil) or similar. Middle High German kegel means “peg or pin used for a game” (such as skittles), but regional use from the 14th century onward also preserve a more general meaning of “peg, cudgel”. The etymology cannot be traced with certainty. The word is a member of a Wortsippe which …

noun:Kehre.tx: From Middle High German kēr, from Old High German kēr. By surface analysis, kehren + -e. Compare English char.

noun:Kelle.tx: From Middle High German kelle, from Old High German kella, of obscure origin. Possibly from Ancient Greek κήλων (kḗlōn).

noun:Keller.tx: From Middle High German keller, from Old High German kellari, from Proto-West Germanic *kellārī (“cellar, storeroom”). See Kellner.

noun:Kerl.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German kerl, from Old Saxon *keril, from Proto-West Germanic *karil. Cognate with Old High German karal. Akin to Dutch kerel, English churl, Old Norse karl, Danish karl.

noun:Kette.tx: From Middle High German keten, ketene, from Old High German ketinna, ketina, from Proto-West Germanic *katinnjā (“chain”).

verb:keuchen.tx: From a conflation of Middle High German kuchen (“to breathe”) (from Proto-Germanic *kuh-) and kīchen (“to breathe hard; pant; gasp; wheeze”), ultimately of imitative origin. Compare Dutch kuchen, English cough.

noun:Keule.tx: From Middle High German kiule, kūle, from Old High German *kiula, from Proto-West Germanic *kiulijā, from Proto-Germanic *kiulijǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *gewl-o- (“vessel; club”), an l-extension of *gew- (“to bend, arch”) (DWDS). Cognate with Middle Low German kü̂le.

noun:Kiel.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German kēl, kil, probably borrowed from Old Norse kjǫlr. Compare Dutch kiel, English keel.

noun:Kieme.tx: 16th century, from Middle Low German kime, kimme. This is most plausibly an alteration of kiwe (“jawbone, gill”) after unrelated kimme (“slit, groove”), whence also German Kimme. The former pertains to kauen (“to chew”) and is cognate with Middle High German kiwe (“jawbone, gill”), Dutch kieuw (“gill”).

noun:Kiesel.tx: From Middle High German kisel, from Old High German kisil, from Proto-West Germanic *kisil, *kesul (“pebble, gravel”).

noun:Kinn.tx: From Middle High German kinne, from Old High German kinni, from Proto-West Germanic *kinnu, from Proto-Germanic *kinnuz, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵénu-, *ǵénus (“chin, jaw, cheek”). Compare Low German Kinn, Dutch kin, English chin, Danish kind, Icelandic kinn.

noun:Kippe.tx: Probably via unattested Middle Low German and Old Saxon forms from Latin cippus (“pole”). The word is attested in early modern German in an Upper German form kipfe and originally meant “top, point”.

noun:Kissen.tx: From Middle High German küssen, from Old High German kussīn, from Proto-West Germanic *kussīn (“cushion, pillow”). The form Kissen with dialectal unrounding was standardised to avoid homophony with küssen (“to kiss”).

noun:Kiste.tx: From Middle High German kiste, from Old High German kista, from Proto-West Germanic *kistu (“chest, box”).

noun:Kitt.tx: From Middle High German küt, küte, from Old High German kuti, quiti, kwiti, from Proto-West Germanic *kwidu, from Proto-Germanic *kweduz.

noun:Kittel.tx: From Middle High German kitel. Further origin uncertain; sometimes derived from Arabic قُطْن (quṭn, “cotton”), but this is doubtful. Cognate with Yiddish קיטל (kitl), Luxembourgish Kiddel, Middle Dutch kedel (modern kiel), Middle Low German kēdel.

noun:Klage.tx: From Middle High German klage, from Old High German klaga.

noun:Klamm.tx: From Middle High German klam, from Old High German klam, modern German Klemme, from verb klemmen, attested regionally since 11th c.

noun:Klammer.tx: From Middle High German klammer, klamer, klamere.

noun:Klang.tx: From Middle High German klanc, from Old High German klang, clanch. Related to klingen. Compare English clank.

noun:Klappe.tx: From the verb klappen (“to flap, flip, fold”) and from Middle Low German klappe, kleppe and with influence of French clapet in technical meanings near “valve”.

noun:Klapper.tx: From Middle High German klapper. Synchronically analyzable as derived from the verb klappern.

noun:Klee.tx: From Middle High German klee, from Old High German chlēo, from Proto-West Germanic *klaiw.

noun:Klasse.tx: Ultimately from Latin classis, probably via French classe.

noun:Krebs.tx: From Middle High German krebȥ, krebeȥ, krebeȥe, from Old High German crebiȥ, krebiȥ, from Proto-West Germanic *krabit, from Proto-Germanic *krabitaz, from Proto-Indo-European *gerbʰ- (“to scratch”), see also Old Prussian gīrbin (“number”), Old Church Slavonic жрѣбии (žrěbii, “lot, tallymark”), Ancient Greek γράφειν (gráphein, “to scratch, etch”), Dutch kreeft. The sense “cancer” is a semantic …

noun:Klinge.tx: From Middle High German klinge, derived from klingen (“to sound”), from the sound of clashing metal; see Old High German chlinga f, chlingo m. Cognate with Middle Low German klinge.

verb:klingen.tx: From Middle High German klingen, Old High German klingan, from Proto-West Germanic *klingan, from Proto-Germanic *klinganą. More at clink.

noun:Klemme.tx: From Middle High German klemme, klemde, or from the verb klemmen.

verb:klemmen.tx: From Middle High German klemmen, from Old High German klemmen, (bi)klemmen, from Proto-West Germanic *klammjan, which could be related to *klimban (“to clamp, clasp, climb onto”).

noun:Klippe.tx: From Middle High German klippe, borrowed from Middle Low German klippe or Middle Dutch clippe, ultimately from the root of Kliff (“cliff”). Cognate with Dutch klip, English cliff.

noun:Kluft.tx: From Old High German kluft, from Proto-Germanic *kluftiz. Compare Dutch klucht, English cleft.

noun:Klumpen.tx: A Low and Central German word, attested in High German texts from the 15th century. From northern Middle High German *klumpe and Middle Low German klumpe, both from Old Saxon *klumpo, from Proto-Germanic *klumpô (“mass, lump, clump; clasp”), from Proto-Indo-European *glembʰ- (“lump, clamp”). Cognate with Dutch klomp (whence English clump), Danish klump, Swedish klump.

noun:Knabe.tx: From Middle High German knabe, from Old High German knabo, chnabo, from Proto-West Germanic *knabō, cognate with English knave.

noun:Knall.tx: Derived from the verb in Middle High German knellen (“to crash, crack, creak”), probably of onomatopoeic origin (lautmalend).

noun:Knäuel.tx: From Middle High German *kniuwel (attested in the form knüel), dissimilation of kliuwel, diminutive of kliuwe, from Old High German kliuwa. Cognate with English clew and clue.

noun:Knast.tx: Through Rotwelsch (thieves’ cant) from Yiddish קנס (knas, “a fine”), from Hebrew קְנָס (qənās, “a fine”).

noun:Knauf.tx: From Middle High German knouf, from Old High German knouf, from Proto-Germanic *knaupaz, one of several kn- words related to *knuttô (“knot”). Cognate with Dutch knoop. Also related with German Knopf, Dutch knop and further with German Knubbel, Dutch knobbel, English knob.

noun:Knebel.tx: From Middle High German knebel, from Old High German knebil.

noun:Kneipe.tx: From kneipen, an archaic variant of kneifen (“to pinch, squeeze”). The noun spread from student slang of Upper Saxony in the later 18th century, possibly picked up from thieves’ cant, and is based on the idea of a crowded pub where people, as it were, squeeze and poke each other. Kneipe became the commonest word for “pub” during the 20th century.

noun:Knick.tx: Deverbal from knicken (“to bend, to fold”).

verb:knicken.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German knicken, from Proto-Germanic *knikkōną (“to fold, snap”), which is partly imitative. Cognate with Dutch knikken.

noun:Kniff.tx: 18th century, from the verb kneifen, after Low German Kneep, from Middle Low German knēp (“trick”). Compare Dutch kneep.

verb:kneifen.tx: Derived from earlier kneipen, from Middle Low German knīpen, from Old Saxon *knīpan, from Proto-West Germanic *knīpan. Cognate with Dutch knijpen. Doublet of kniepen (“to blink”), a more recent borrowing from modern Low German. The form with -f- is an adaptation to the High German consonantism, for which there may have been rare antetypes in northern dialects of Central German, but which was …

noun:Knirps.tx: Cognate with Low German knirfix, Middle English närvel, maybe also with Swabian knorp, Dutch knorf. Sense “umbrella” from a brand name, referring to the small size of the (folded) umbrella.

noun:Knöchel.tx: From Middle High German knöchel, from Old High German *knuchil, from Proto-West Germanic *knukil (“knuckle”).

noun:Knoten.tx: From Middle High German knote, knode, from Old High German knoto, knodo. The two forms are probably variants based on Grammatischer Wechsel. The form with -t- (from Proto-Germanic *-d-) was predominant in East Central German, that with -d- (from Proto-Germanic *-þ-) in Upper German. Incidentally, this situation explains the lengthened vowel in the standardized form (lengthening being blocked …

noun:Knospe.tx: Akin to the noun Knopf; cognate with Hunsrik Knosb, Luxembourgish Knosp

noun:Knolle.tx: From Middle High German knolle, Old High German *chnollo, from Proto-Germanic *knudan-, *knudla-, *knulla- (“lump”), possibly related to Old English cnotta. Cognate with Old English cnoll, Dutch knol, English knoll.

verb:knüpfen.tx: From Middle High German knüpfen, from Old High German knupfen; related to Knopf.

verb:kneten.tx: From Middle High German knëten, from Old High German knëtan, from Proto-West Germanic *knedan, from Proto-Germanic *knudaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gnet- (“to press together”).

noun:Knüppel.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German knüppel. Akin to Knopf (“button”).

noun:Köder.tx: From Middle High German quërder, from Old High German quërdar, from Proto-Germanic *kwerþraz (“bait”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷérh₃-tro-s, from the root *gʷerh₃- (“to devour”).

noun:Koje.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German kōje, from Middle Dutch coye, koye, from Latin cavea. Compare Dutch kooi.

noun:Kolben.tx: From Middle High German kolbe (“club”), from Old High German kolbo, cholpo, from Proto-West Germanic *kolbō, extension of Proto-Germanic *kulbaz (“round object”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“to form into a ball”). Cognate with Dutch kolf, whence probably English golf.

noun:Korn.tx: From Middle High German korn, from Old High German korn, from Proto-West Germanic *korn, from Proto-Germanic *kurną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵr̥h₂nóm.

noun:Körper.tx: From Middle High German korper, körper, körpel, from Latin corpor-, inflected stem of corpus. The word displaced first the predecessor of German Leiche, Leichnam (now “corpse”) and later on Leib (now dated, literary, religious). Doublet of Korpus, Korps. The umlaut remained rare until the 16th century. Its derivation from the -i- in Latin corporis, corpori seems unlikely in such a late borrowing. …

noun:Kosten.tx: From Middle High German koste, kost. From Medieval Latin costus, costa. Ultimately from the Latin verb constare. Older singular forms were found in Kost f, Koste f, Kost m, and Kosten m.

noun:Krach.tx: From Middle High German krach, from Old High German krah, krac.

noun:Kraft.tx: From Middle High German kraft, from Old High German kraft, from Proto-West Germanic *kraftu, from Proto-Germanic *kraftuz (strength, power). Cognate with Dutch kracht, Low German Kracht, English craft, Danish kraft.

noun:Kragen.tx: From Middle High German krage (“neck”), from Proto-Germanic *kragô (“throat”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *gʷrogʰ-. Cognate with Hunsrik Kraa, Dutch kraag, probably also English craw; see the English for more (DWDS).

noun:Krähe.tx: From Middle High German krā, krāe, krawe, from Old High German krāwa, kraja, krāha, from Proto-West Germanic *krāā, from Proto-Germanic *krēǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *ger- (“to scream, cry, creak”). Compare Dutch kraai, English crow, Plautdietsch Krauj.

noun:Krampf.tx: From Middle High German kramph, cramph, from Old High German krampho, chrampho, chramph, from Proto-West Germanic *krampu, from Proto-Germanic *krampō (“cramp, clasp”). More at cramp.

noun:Kran.tx: From Middle High German krane, from Old High German krano (“crane”), from Proto-West Germanic *kranō, from Proto-Germanic *kranô (“crane”). The word was used metaphorically for the lifting device due to the similar appearance of the bird’s neck and head. This metaphorical use is first attested in Middle Dutch krane, and thence spread to several European languages (compare English crane, French …

noun:Kranich.tx: From Middle High German kranech, from Old High German chranuh, from Proto-West Germanic *kranuk, diminutive of Proto-Germanic *kranô (“crane”).

noun:Kranz.tx: From Middle High German kranz, from Old High German kranz, of uncertain origin, but probably related to the root of Kringel (“loop, curl”). An exclusively High German word (compare e.g. Luxembourgish Kranz, Vilamovian kraonc). From Middle High German are borrowed Dutch krans, Danish krans, and other Scandinavian forms.

verb:kratzen.tx: From Middle High German kratzen, from Old High German krazzōn, chrazzōn, from Proto-Germanic *krattōną, from Proto-Indo-European *gred- (“to scrape”); compare Albanian gërresë (“rasp, scraper”).

noun:Krawall.tx: Unknown. Perhaps borrowed from Late Latin charavallium (“noise and clamor at a wedding”), or from Old French chalivali (“noise from pots and pans”) or charivali (compare French charivari), from Late Latin caribaria or Late Latin carivaria, ultimately from Ancient Greek καρηβάρεια (karēbáreia, “heaviness of the head, dizziness, headache”), from κάρη (kárē, “head”) and βαρύς (barús, “heavy”).

noun:Krawatte.tx: Borrowed from French cravate. Compare English cravat and Spanish corbata. Doublet of Kroate (“Croat”).

noun:Kreis.tx: From Middle High German kreiȥ, from Old High German kreiȥ, from Proto-West Germanic *krait, from Proto-Germanic *kraitaz. Compare the semantic development of the descendants of Proto-Slavic *krajь (eg. Czech kraj, Russian край (kraj)), *okrǫgъ (eg. Polish okręg, Serbo-Croatian okrug).

noun:Kreisel.tx: From Middle High German kriusel, derived from krūs, whence modern kraus (“frizzy, curly”). Doublet of Kräusel (“frizzle, squiggle”). The sense “spinning top” was borrowed from cognate Middle Low German krü̂sel into East Central German, whence it spread in the written language. The unrounded form Kreisel was later standardised due to association with etymologically unrelated Kreis (“circle”). It …

noun:Krippe.tx: From Middle High German krippe, from Old High German krippa, from Proto-West Germanic *kribbjā, from Proto-Germanic *kribjǭ (“crib, wickerwork”). Doublet of Kribbe ("breakwater").

noun:Kropf.tx: From Middle High German kropf, from Old High German kropf, from Proto-Germanic *kruppaz. Cognate with English crop, which see.

noun:Krücke.tx: From Middle High German krucke, krücke, from Old High German krucka, from Proto-West Germanic *krukkju, from Proto-Germanic *krukjō (“crutch, staff”), from Proto-Indo-European *grewg- (“wrinkle, bend”), from *ger- (“to turn, bend”).

noun:Krug.tx: From Middle High German kruoc, from Old High German kruog, from Proto-West Germanic *krōgu, from Proto-Germanic *krōguz. Immediate cognates are Middle Dutch croech, Old English crōg, of obscure origin. Possibly from a Proto-Indo-European root shared with Old Armenian կարաս (karas, “pitcher, large jar”), Ancient Greek κρωσσός (krōssós, “pitcher”), but the phonetics are problematic. Also compare …

noun:Krume.tx: From Middle High German (Central German) krume, reinforced by Middle Low German krume, krōme. See Krümel for more.

noun:Krüppel.tx: From Middle High German krüppel, krüpel, borrowed from Middle Low German kröpel, from Old Saxon krupil (“crippled, paralyzed”), from Proto-West Germanic *kruppil. Cognate with Dutch kreupel, English cripple. See there for more.

adj:krumm.tx: From Middle High German krump, from Old High German krump, from Proto-West Germanic *krump, from Proto-Germanic *krumbaz.

noun:Kruste.tx: From Old High German krusta, borrowed from Latin crusta.

noun:Küste.tx: From early modern Dutch kust(e) (“coast”), from Old French coste (“side; coast”), from Latin costa (“rib”). Compare modern French côte, English coast.

noun:Kuckuck.tx: From Middle High German kukkuk, kukuk, gugug; ultimately onomatopoeic. Compare German Low German Kukuuk, Dutch koekoek, Middle English cukkuk, gokkouȝ (modern English cuckoo).

adj:kühn.tx: From Middle High German küene, from Old High German kuoni, from Proto-Germanic *kōniz. Cognate with Dutch koen, English keen.

adj:kühl.tx: From Middle High German küele, Old High German kuoli, from Proto-West Germanic *kōl(ī), from Proto-Germanic *kōluz, *kōlaz, from Proto-Indo-European *gel-. Cognate with Dutch koel, English cool. Doublet of cool.

noun:Kunde.tx: From Middle High German kunde, from Old High German cundo, from Proto-West Germanic *kunþō. Cognate with Old English cūþa and Middle Dutch konde (“acquaintance, friend”).

noun:Kürbis.tx: From Middle High German kürbiȥ, from Old High German kurbiȥ, from Proto-West Germanic *kurbit. Cognate with Luxembourgish Kürbis, Yiddish קירבעס (kirbes).

noun:Kraftwerk.tx: From Kraft (“power”) + Werk (“factory”). Cognate with Danish kraftværk, Norwegian and Swedish kraftverk.

noun:Karpfen.tx: From Middle High German karpfe, from Old High German karpho. The Central German form Karpe(n) was widespread in earlier modern German (well into the 19th century and well into Upper German territory). This may be a reason why the form has not been simplified to *Karfen, it being the only word in modern standard German in which -rpf- has not been simplified to -rf-. Further origin unsettled; …

noun:Krapfen.tx: From Middle High German krapfe, from Old High German krapho. Cognate with English grape.

noun:Kürze.tx: Inherited from Middle High German kürze, from Old High German kurzī; analyzable as kurz + -e.

adj:kahl.tx: From Middle High German kal (inflected kalwe), from Old High German kalo, chalo, from Proto-West Germanic *kalu, from Proto-Germanic *kalwaz (“naked, bald”), from Proto-Indo-European *gelH- (“naked, bald”). The form kahl (instead of *kalb) is based on the Middle High German uninflected stem. However, the lengthened vowel points to influence by varieties that reduce -lw- to -l- even in open …

noun:Kühle.tx: Inherited from Middle High German küele, from Old High German kuolī, from Proto-West Germanic *kōlī. Analysable as kühl + -e.

adj:klug.tx: From Middle High German kluoc, which was borrowed via the Lower Rhineland from Middle Low German klōk and Middle Dutch cloec, from Proto-Germanic *klōkaz. Compare Old Norse klókr, and dialectal Dutch kloek. In Upper German dialects, the final [k]-sound after a long vowel was naturally interpreted as underlying /ɡ/. This form then also spread back northwards, though some northern Central German …

adj:karg.tx: From Middle High German karc, from Old High German karag, charag.

adj:kraus.tx: From Middle High German krūs (“frizzy”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *kruzlǭ (“bent or crooked object, curl”), of unknown origin; possibly from Pre-Germanic *grus-, contracted from Proto-Indo-European *gurus- (“twist, curl”), same source as Persian گرس (gors, “braid of hair”). Related to English curl and Dutch krullen (“to curl”).

noun:Kapitel.tx: In the sense of “clerical body” inherited from Middle High German kapitel, capittel, from Latin capitulum. In the sense of “text section” a later borrowing from the same source (ca. 1500). Occasional Old High German kapital, kapitula had no sustained continuation in Middle High German.

verb:kitzeln.tx: From Middle High German kitzeln, from Old High German kizzilōn, from Proto-West Germanic *kitilōn. Cognate with Hunsrik kitzle, Luxembourgish këddelen, English kittle.

verb:klopfen.tx: From Middle High German klopfen, from Old High German klophōn, clophōn, from Proto-West Germanic *kloppōn, from Proto-Germanic *kluppōną. Cognate with Dutch kloppen. See also the informal doublet kloppen (“to thump, beat, fight”).

verb:knurren.tx: Imitative of deep sounds. Compare Dutch knorren.

verb:kriechen.tx: Middle High German kriechen, from Old High German kriohhan, from Proto-West Germanic *kreukan, from Proto-Germanic *kreukaną.

verb:kämpfen.tx: From Middle High German kempfen, from Old High German *kempfan, from Proto-West Germanic *kampijan.

noun:Kollektion.tx: 18th century, from Latin collēctiō, in part through French collection.

noun:Kabel.tx: From Middle High German kabel, which is borrowed via Middle Low German from Middle Dutch cabel (“thick rope”), itself from northern French câble. The contemporary sense is from English cable, which see for more.

noun:Kadenz.tx: Borrowed from Italian cadenza, from Latin cadentia.

noun:Kakadu.tx: Borrowed from Dutch kaketoe, from Malay kakaktua.

noun:Kalauer.tx: After the city Calau, influenced by French calembour.

noun:Krankheit.tx: From Middle High German krancheit, krankeit. By surface analysis, krank + -heit; compare Alemannic German Chranket, Luxembourgish Krankheet. Eclipsed non-native Middle High German malāze (“sickness, disease”), ultimately from Latin.

phrase:Kopf und Kragen.tx: Literally, “head and collar”. Compare English neck for a similar semantic change.

adj:komisch.tx: Early 16th century in the sense “comedic”, directly from Latin com(icus) + -isch, from Ancient Greek κωμικός (kōmikós). The broader sense “funny” since the 17th century under influence of French comique. The sense “strange” was derived thence (as in English funny).

noun:Königreich.tx: From Middle High German künicriche, from Old High German kuningrīhhi, from Proto-West Germanic *kuningarīkī, from Proto-Germanic *kuningarīkiją. Equivalent to König (“king”) + Reich (“empire”). Compare Dutch koninkrijk, Danish kongerige, Old English cyningrice.

noun:Kanonenfutter.tx: From Kanone (“cannon”) + Futter (“fodder”). Attested in 1796 (see quote below). The formation may have been inspired by English food for powder (Shakespeare, Henry IV, Part 1), but this is uncertain. The earliest translations by Wieland (1764), Eschenburg (1779), and Schlegel (1800) all translate the phrase literally as Futter für Pulver. Ortlepp’s version (1839) appears to be the first to use Kanonenfutter instead.

noun:Kanone.tx: Borrowed from Italian cannone (“large tube”), a derivation of canna (“tube”).

noun:Knappe.tx: From Middle High German knappe, from Old High German knappo, from Proto-West Germanic *knappō.

noun:Königin.tx: From Middle High German künigin, from Old High German chuningin, from Proto-West Germanic *kuningini, equivalent to König + -in. Cognate with West Frisian keninginne.

adj:klamm.tx: From Middle High German klam (“narrow, tight, solid”), from Old High German klam, from or related to Proto-West Germanic *klaimijan (“to smear with clay”). The modern sense is chiefly Central and Low German (Middle Low German klam). Cognate with Dutch klam. Also related with English clammy.

verb:klagen.tx: From Middle High German klagen, from Old High German klagōn, from Proto-West Germanic *klagōn (“to lament, complain”).

noun:Kaninchen.tx: From Middle Low German kanīneken, diminutive of kanīn, konīn, itself probably through Middle Dutch connijn from Old French connin, northern variant of connil, from Latin cunīculus. Analysable as Kanin + -chen. Compare English cony.

noun:Kaulquappe.tx: 15th century; from Middle High German kūle (modern Kaule) "hollow, pond" and *kwappō (“type of fresh-water fish”) (more at *žaba).

noun:Katzengold.tx: Middle High German katzengolt, Katze + -n- + Gold, literally “cat's gold”

noun:Kapitän.tx: From Middle High German kapitān, borrowed (13th c.) in the military sense from Old French capitaine (“leader”), from Late Latin capitāneus. The nautical sense (15th c.) follows Italian capitano. The sport sense (early 20th c.) follows English captain.

noun:Kobold.tx: From Middle High German kobe (“shed, sty”) (modern Koben) + *holt (“goblin”), from hold (“friendly, gracious”), a euphemistic way of referring to the mischievous beings, from Proto-Germanic *hulþaz (“inclined, favorable”). Related to Dutch kabouter. Typologically compare with English the good folk.

noun:Kaktus.tx: Borrowed from Latin cactus, from Ancient Greek κάκτος (káktos, “cardoon”), of pre-Greek origin.

noun:Knöterich.tx: From Knote (an early form of Knoten (“knot”)) + -rich.

verb:kippen.tx: An originally Low German and Central German word of uncertain origin. Possibly derived from Kippe (etymology 1).

noun:Konzentrationslager.tx: From Konzentration (“concentration”) + -s- + Lager (“camp”), a calque of English concentration camp.

noun:Komet.tx: From Middle High German comēte, from Old French comete, from Latin comēta.

adj:kommunal.tx: From Latin communalis. By surface analysis, Kommune + -al.

adj:konkret.tx: Borrowed from Latin concrētus, past participle of concrescere (com- + crescere).

adv:konkret.tx: Borrowed from Latin concrētus, past participle of concrescere (com- + crescere).

adj:kross.tx: From German Low German and West Central German dialects. Onomatopoeic. A certain relation with Kruste (“crust”) is not ruled out, but less likely since the relevant dialects invariably have metathesis of -r- in this noun (Korst, Kursch, etc.).

noun:Karotte.tx: Borrowed from French carotte, from Latin carōta, from Ancient Greek κᾰρωτόν (kărōtón).

noun:Kohlrabi.tx: From Italian cavoli rape, plural of cavolo rapa. The first element was altered after Kohl (“cabbage”), which is cognate with the Italian through Latin caulis. Compare Hunsrik Kohlraab.

noun:Kristall.tx: From Middle High German kristal, kristalle, from Old High German cristalla, from Latin crystallum, from Ancient Greek κρύσταλλος (krústallos, “ice”). Cognate with Vilamovian kryśtaoł.

verb:knabbern.tx: Borrowed from German Low German knabbeln, knabbern, which appears to be an iterative verbal formation related to knapp (“scarce, barely”), with onomatopoeic reinforcement. Compare Dutch knabbelen. May be related to Rotwelsch Knapp (“bread”).

noun:Kurs.tx: Derived from Latin cursus. Cognate with Russian курс (kurs), French cours, French course, English course etc. Doublet of Korso.

noun:Knecht.tx: Inherited from Middle High German knëht, from Old High German knëht, from Proto-West Germanic *kneht.

noun:Kamerad.tx: Borrowed from French camarade in the 16th century, ultimately from Latin camera (“chamber”); see Kammer, from Ancient Greek καμάρα (kamára).

noun:Kamin.tx: From Middle High German kamîn, from Old High German kemîn, from Latin camīnus. Compare English chimney.

noun:Kloster.tx: From Middle High German klōster, from Old High German klōstar, borrowed from Vulgar Latin *clōstrum, Medieval Latin claustrum.

noun:Klugheit.tx: From Middle High German kluocheit. By surface analysis, klug + -heit.

adj:kommerziell.tx: Borrowed from French commercial (“of, or pertaining to commerce”), from Late Latin commercialis, from Latin commercium.

verb:kreischen.tx: From Middle High German krīschen, from Old High German *krīskan, from Proto-West Germanic *krīskan, from *krīskaną (“to cry out, shout”), from Proto-Indo-European *grey- (“to shout”). According to Pfeifer, this is an extension of Proto-Indo-European *gerh₂- (“to cry hoarsely”), which makes it cognate with dated/obsolete German kreißen (“to cry in pain, give birth”). Cognate with Dutch krijsen, …

noun:Karton.tx: Borrowed from French carton, from Italian cartone. Doublet of Cartoon.

noun:Kojote.tx: From Spanish coyote, from Classical Nahuatl coyōtl.

noun:Kommission.tx: Borrowed from Latin commissiō (“sending together; commission”) (genitive singular commissiōnis).

noun:Komitee.tx: Borrowed from French comité. First attested in the 18th century.

noun:Kunstwerk.tx: From Kunst (“art”) + -werk (“-work”). Cognate with Swedish konstverk, Danish kunstværk, Dutch kunstwerk, Norwegian kunstverk.

noun:Kommentar.tx: Borrowed from Latin commentārius, commentārium m (“notebook, commentary”).

noun:Konfetti.tx: Borrowed from Italian confetti, plural of confetto (“confection”), reinterpreted as a singular (compare Spaghetti).

noun:Karneval.tx: From Italian carnevale, from the Latin phrase carnem levāre, to put away meat.

noun:Kordel.tx: Borrowed from French cordelle, diminutive of corde (“rope”).

noun:Karikatur.tx: From Italian caricare (“to load”) and caricatura.

verb:kühlen.tx: From Middle High German küelen, from Old High German kuolōn, chuolen, from Proto-Germanic *kōlōną, *kōlēną, related to *kalaną (“to be cold”). Equivalent to kühl + -en. Cognate with Hunsrik kiele, Luxembourgish killen, Dutch koelen, Saterland Frisian köile, English cool (verb), Swedish kyla.

noun:Koffein.tx: From earlier Kaffein, changed under influence of Latin coffē̆a.

noun:Klaustrophobie.tx: Borrowed from French claustrophobie, from Latin claustrum (“a shut in place”) + -phobie.

noun:Kasse.tx: Borrowed from Italian cassa, from Latin capsa.

verb:kassieren.tx: 17th century, from Kasse (“treasury, cash register”) + -ieren. The sense “take away” may be partially influenced by etymology 2 below.

noun:Kaleidoskop.tx: Borrowed from English kaleidoscope; see there for more.

noun:Katastrophe.tx: From Latin catastropha (“turning-point of an action, catastrophe”), from Ancient Greek καταστροφή (katastrophḗ, “overturning”).

noun:Konzert.tx: Borrowed in the 17th century from Italian concerto, ultimately from Latin concertō (“to dispute”).

verb:kriegen.tx: From Middle High German kriegen (“to war, to conquer property or land”). Verbalisation of Krieg (“war”). Cognate to Bavarian kriagn, Dutch krijgen, Hunsrik krien.

noun:Kompass.tx: 15th century, from Italian compasso (in which the sense “compass” is now rare and considered an anglicism, though it was usual in older Italian).

noun:Kategorie.tx: From Late Latin catēgoria (compare Yiddish קאַטעגאָריע (kategorye)), from Ancient Greek κατηγορία (katēgoría).

noun:Kapelle.tx: From Middle High German kappelle, kapelle, from Old High German kappella, kapella, from Late Latin and Vulgar Latin cappella (“chapel”).

noun:Koloss.tx: 16th century semi-learned borrowing from Latin colossus, from Ancient Greek κολοσσός (kolossós).

noun:Konsument.tx: Borrowed from Latin cōnsūmēns (“consuming”) (genitive singular cōnsūmentis).

noun:Kanne.tx: From Middle High German kanne, Old High German channa, from Proto-Germanic *kannǭ. Cognate with Old Norse kanna, Old English canne, English can, French canette (“small can”), Gothic *𐌺𐌰𐌽𐌽𐍉 (*kannō).

noun:Korrektur.tx: 16th century, borrowed from Latin correctura (literally “that which shall correct”). At first used in the context of printing for lists of errata.

noun:Kindheit.tx: From Middle High German kintheit, from Old High German kindheit (also kindesheit), equivalent to Kind + -heit.

noun:Kanal.tx: 15th century, from Italian canale, from Latin canalis. The broadcasting sense is a semantic loan from English channel.

noun:Koriander.tx: From Middle High German koriander, from earlier koliander, from Old High German kullantar, kullintar (9th c.), from Latin coliandrum, variant of coriandrum. An early borrowing as Proto-West Germanic *kulljandr is possible, though the only cognate is Old English cellender. The relatinization of the German form was gradual and began already in Old High German.

noun:Kostüm.tx: First borrowed in the early 18th century directly from Italian costume, which see. Later influenced by French costume, itself also from the Italian.

noun:Knute.tx: Borrowed from Russian кнут (knut), from Old East Slavic кнутъ (knutŭ), from Old Norse knútr (“knot”).

noun:Karte.tx: From Late Middle High German karte (“stiff sheet of paper”), from Old French carte, from Latin charta, from Ancient Greek χάρτης (khártēs). Compare Dutch kaart, English card, Yiddish קאָרט (kort), Low German Kaart, Koort. Doublet of Charta and Karton. See also Charter.

noun:Kleie.tx: From Middle High German klīwe, klīe, from Old High German klīwa, klīa, klīga. The further origin is unclear. It might stem from Proto-Indo-European *gley- (“to smear, glue”) but this is difficult due to semantic reasons.

noun:Kalorie.tx: Borrowed from French calorie, from Latin calor.

noun:Kreuzer.tx: From Middle High German kriuzære; analyzable as Kreuz + -er, from the cross that was stamped on this coin.

noun:Kalle.tx: From Yiddish כּלה (kale, “bride”), from Hebrew כַּלָּה (kalá, “bride”).

noun:Karo.tx: Borrowed from French carreau. Doublet of Quadrat.

noun:Kontroverse.tx: Learned borrowing from Latin contrōversia, cognate to obsolete English controverse.

noun:Katakombe.tx: 18th century, from Italian catacomba, from Latin catacumbae.

noun:Karre.tx: A chiefly Central and Low German form (vis-à-vis Upper German Karren). From Middle Low German karre f and northern Middle High German karre f, from Old Saxon karra and Old High German karra, from Latin carrus (“cart”), from Gaulish *karros. Compare Dutch kar, English car, Swedish kärra. Doublet of Ross.

noun:Koalition.tx: Borrowed in from English coalition, ultimatlely from Latin coalitiō.

verb:klatschen.tx: Onomatopoeic. Compare Dutch kletsen and English clash.

adj:kriminell.tx: From Late Latin criminalis, from Latin crimen, via French criminel.

noun:Komfort.tx: 19th century, partly from English comfort (hence the -m-), partly from French confort (hence the mute -t), both from Old French confort, from conforter, from Latin confortare.

noun:Kurde.tx: From the name in Kurdish, but of unknown ultimate meaning. More at Kurds.

noun:Kitz.tx: From Middle High German kiz, kitze, from Old High German kizzī, kizzīn, from Proto-Germanic *kittīną (“goatling, kid”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *gidʰ- (“kid, goatling, little goat”). Cognate with Low German kitte, English chit. Related also to English kid, Danish kid, Swedish kid.

noun:Kefir.tx: Borrowed from Russian кефи́р (kefír); see that entry for more.

noun:Kicker.tx: From English kicker. By surface analysis, kicken + -er.

noun:Kaufmann.tx: Historically from Middle High German koufman, from Old High German koufman, from Proto-West Germanic *kaupamann, equivalent to kaufen + Mann.

verb:kündigen.tx: From Middle High German kündigen in the sense “to make known” derived from kündic now kundig; in the contractual termination sense not part of regular vocabulary before the 19th century and clipped from aufkündigen, abkündigen, verkündigen.

noun:Kakerlake.tx: Back-formation from the plural Kakerlaken of Kakerlak, which is the more original form of the word. The latter from Dutch kakkerlak.

noun:Kenntnis.tx: From Middle High German kenntnisse, kantnisse, kantnüsse, kantnusse, kantnust, kannusse, equivalent to kennen + -t + -nis. Cognate with Hunsrik Kenntniss, Luxembourgish Kenntnes, Yiddish קענטעניש (kentenish).

noun:Kasper.tx: Byform of the name German Kaspar, via Biblical Hebrew גִּזְבָּר (gizbar) from Classical Syriac ܓܙܒܪܐ (gēzaḇrā), from Old Persian *ganzabarah, from Old Median *ganǰabarah. Compare Bavarian Kasperl.

noun:Kapital.tx: Borrowed from Italian capitale (“(economic) capital”), from Latin capitālis.

noun:Konsum.tx: From earlier Consumo, borrowed from Italian consumo, from Latin cōnsūmō.

noun:Krokus.tx: Learned borrowing from Latin crocus, from Ancient Greek κρόκος (krókos).

noun:Konsulat.tx: Borrowed from Latin cōnsulātus. By surface analysis, Konsul + -at.

noun:Kanu.tx: 16th century, borrowed from Spanish canoa, from Taíno *kanowa. Pronunciation and spelling were influenced by English canoe and French canot (cf. Kanute).

noun:Klaviatur.tx: Artificial creation of the loanword-ridden 17th century after Klavier, parallelly inventing New Latin clāviatūra.

noun:Kasus.tx: Borrowed from Latin cāsus, from cadō (“to fall”).

noun:Kutte.tx: From Middle High German kutte (“monk habit”), from Medieval Latin cotta (“undercoat, tunic”), from Proto-Germanic *kuttô (“cowl, woolen cloth, coat”).

verb:kiffen.tx: From Kif + -en or perhaps after French kiffer. Ultimately from Moroccan Arabic كيف (kīf), from Arabic كَيْف (kayf, “opiate”).

noun:Konfitüre.tx: Borrowed from French confiture. Compare Switzerland Italian confittura.

noun:Kavalier.tx: Borrowed from Italian cavalier, from Old French chevalier, from Late Latin caballārius (“horse rider”). Early loans into Middle High German, as cavali(e)r, are recorded for the 14th century, but remained without direct continuants. Renewed loan in the later 16th century, as Caval(l)ier, Cavaglier, Cavalierer , at the time with Italian plural Cavalieri, but in the 17th century replaced with the …

adj:komplett.tx: From French complet, from Latin completus. Cognate with Hunsrik kumplett.

noun:Klassiker.tx: From French (auteur) classique + -er or, according to Kluge, directly from Latin classicus (scriptor). Initially describing specifically authors of the classical antiquity, with the sense broadening over time. By surface analysis, Klassik + -er.

adj:köstlich.tx: From Middle High German kostlich, kostelich. By surface analysis, kosten (“to taste”) + -lich.

noun:Konkurrenz.tx: From Latin concurrentia (“concurrence; competition”). Compare English concurrence.

noun:Kurier.tx: From Middle High German kurier, kurrier, from French courrier.

adj:komfortabel.tx: 19th century, from English comfortable and French confortable. Equivalent to Komfort + -abel.

noun:Kommandeur.tx: Borrowed from French commandeur. Doublet of Kommodore.

noun:Karawane.tx: 15th century, from Italian caravana (older form of carovana), from Persian کاروان (kârvân).

noun:Kreuzung.tx: From kreuzen + -ung; cognate with Hunsrik Kreizung.

noun:Karnickel.tx: From earlier German Low German Kanickel, from a variant of Middle Low German kanīn, from Middle French connin (see Kaninchen). The form is probably based on Latin cunīculus. The -r- might have entered the word from the Brandenburg area, where non-rhotic and strongly rhotic Low German dialects neighboured. The word was probably pronounced with [äː], a sound close to the northern Brandenburg …

noun:Kriterium.tx: Borrowed from Latin critērium, critērion, from Ancient Greek κριτήριον (kritḗrion).

noun:Kuhfladen.tx: From Kuh (“cow”) + Fladen (“flat cake”), literally “cow flathe/flan”.

verb:klappen.tx: A Central and Low German verb, from Middle Low German klappen, from Old Saxon *klappōn, probably from Proto-West Germanic *klappōn, from Proto-Germanic *klappōną. Cognate with Dutch klappen, English clap, Middle High German klapfen (“clapping sound”). Also related with German klaffen (“to be wide open”), and compare kloppen. See also klappern, a derivative of the Middle Low German term.

noun:Kredithai.tx: From Kredit (“loan”) + Hai (“shark”), a calque of English loan shark.

noun:Kolonne.tx: 18th century, from French colonne, from Latin columna. Doublet of Kolumne (“newspaper column”).

noun:Kalkül.tx: Ca. 1700, borrowed from French calcul, from Latin calculus.

noun:Krake.tx: From Norwegian Kraken, definite singular of krake (“sea monster”).

noun:Kaskade.tx: From earlier Cascade (17th century), from French cascade, from Italian cascata, from cascare (“to fall”), from Vulgar Latin *casicāre, from Latin cadō (“to fall”).

noun:Kavallerie.tx: Borrowed from French cavalerie, from Italian cavalleria.

noun:Koteletten.tx: 19th century, from French côtelettes (“sideburns”, literally “cutlets”), humorously after the form, invoking the idea of two cutlets glued to the sides of the face. In French an exclusively informal and now apparently archaic use.

noun:Kaschmir.tx: Borrowed from Hindi [Term?] / Urdu [Term?]; see Kashmir for more.

noun:Kirmes.tx: From Middle High German kirmesse, contraction of kirche (“church”) + messe, misse, from Old High German kirihha + messe (“mass”), + Latin missa, referring to annual solemn masses on the anniversaries of the consecration of village churches (contemporary Kirchweihfest), which developed into major village festivals. Compare the same in Dutch kermis.

noun:Knüller.tx: 20th century. Perhaps from knüllen + -er, where the verb would be used in its obsolete sense “to hit, bump” (compare Schlager), hence probably following dialectal usage or Yiddish קנעלן (kneln). Alternatively it may be a blend of Knaller + Brüller.

noun:Kapsel.tx: From Late Middle High German kapsel, from Latin capsula (“small box or chest”), from Latin capsa (“box, case”), from Latin capiō (“to capture, to seize”).

verb:kandidieren.tx: From Kandidat + -ieren. First attested in the 19th century.

noun:Kürschner.tx: Inherited from Middle High German kürsenære, from Old High German kursināri, derived from kursina, a borrowing from Proto-Slavic *kъrzьno. Equivalent to obsolete Kürsen, Kürschen (“fur coat / furcoat”) + -er.

verb:kreuzigen.tx: From Old High German kruzigōn, also the source of Dutch kruisigen.

noun:Kapazität.tx: From Latin capācitās (“capability; capacity”), from Latin capāx (“large, capacious”), from Latin capiō (“to hold, contain”); compare kapieren, Kapsel.

noun:Kornblume.tx: From Korn (“corn”) + Blume (“flower”). Cognate with Hunsrik Kornblumm, Luxembourgish Karblumm.

adj:kompakt.tx: From French compact, from Latin compactus.

noun:Kajüte.tx: From Middle Low German kajüte, which is probably borrowed from Middle Dutch kayhute, though the latter is attested somewhat later. Further origin unsettled; traditionally held to be of Old French origin, according to Watkins, possibly a mix of cabane + hutte. Compare modern Dutch kajuit.

noun:Konjunktur.tx: 17th century, from Medieval Latin coniunctūra, from coniunctus (“linked”). Originally an astrological term for a kind of constellation, it developed the economic sense in the 18th century. Similar uses in other European languages (French conjoncture, Italian congiuntura) appear to be younger and thus semantic loans from German.

verb:kontrollieren.tx: Borrowed from French contrôler. The sense “to control” is a semantic loan from English control acquired in the 20th century.

noun:Katheter.tx: Borrowed from Latin catheter, from Ancient Greek καθετήρ (kathetḗr).

verb:korrigieren.tx: From Middle High German corrigieren, from Latin corrigere.

noun:Kuli.tx: Borrowed from Hindi क़ुली (qulī) and Urdu قلی (qulī, “hired laborer”), possibly from Ottoman Turkish قول (kul, “servant”).

noun:Kleidung.tx: From Middle High German kleidunge, from kleiden (“to clothe”), from Kleid, from Old High German *kleid, from Proto-Germanic *klaiþą (“cloth”). Cognate with Dutch kleding, English clothing.

noun:Kaplan.tx: From Middle High German kaplān, kappelān, from Medieval Latin cappellānus.

noun:Kreuzfahrt.tx: Middle High German kriuzevart. By surface analysis, Kreuz + Fahrt.

adj:kryptisch.tx: From Late Latin crypticus, with assimilation to native suffix -isch, from Ancient Greek κρυπτικός (kruptikós). Cognate to English cryptic.

noun:Kathedrale.tx: From Kathedralkirche, from Latin ecclesia cathedralis.

noun:Kork.tx: Via Middle Low German or Dutch kurk from early modern Middle Dutch corc, itself from Spanish corcho.

noun:Kaufhaus.tx: From Middle High German koufhūs, from Old High German koufhūs. Equivalent to kaufen (“to buy”) + Haus (“house”).

noun:Kation.tx: Borrowed from English cation, indirectly from Ancient Greek κατα- (kata-, “downwards”) + ἰόν (ión, “wandering”) because cations wander towards the cathode (the place of lower electrical potential).

noun:Kuriosum.tx: From Latin cūriōsum, neuter singular of cūriōsus.

noun:Klabautermann.tx: Borrowed from German Low German [Term?]. Without doubt related, either originally or secondarily, to Dutch kabouter(man). Further etymology unsettled. Several roots seem to have influenced the word phonetically and semantically, it being difficult to determine the oldest form. Assumed influences include: * Middle Dutch cobbout (“goblin”), cognate of German Kobold. * Low German klatern, klattern, …

adj:kursiv.tx: 17th century, backformation from Kursive, from Latin (scriptura) cursiva. The adjective is mainly a term of printing in German, but the noun Kursive is also common for (styles of) cursive handwriting.

verb:klingeln.tx: From Middle High German klingelen, from Old High German klingilōn. Equivalent to klingen + -eln (iterative suffix).

noun:Kongruenz.tx: Borrowed from Latin congruentia, from congruēns, the present active participle of congruō (“to unite, combine, agree”).

adj:kund.tx: From Middle High German kunt, from Old High German kund, from Proto-West Germanic *kunþ, from Proto-Germanic *kunþaz, originally a past participle of *kunnaną.

noun:Köter.tx: Borrowed from Low German Köter, from Middle Low German kȫter. Standard use since the 18th century. Further origin uncertain. Perhaps imitative of panting.

noun:Koryphäe.tx: Borrowed from Ancient Greek κορυφαῖος (koruphaîos, “leader”), from κορυφή (koruphḗ, “top of the head”).

adj:künftig.tx: From Middle High German kümftec, Old High German kumftīg,, equivalent to Kunft + -ig.

adv:künftig.tx: From Middle High German kümftec, Old High German kumftīg,, equivalent to Kunft + -ig.

noun:Kammerjäger.tx: Compound of Kammer (“chamber”) + Jäger (“hunter”). The word originally meant "princely huntsman", but was humorously reinterpreted as "exterminator" (someone who "hunts" in a private "chamber"). This reinterpretation began in German Low German [Term?] and was later standardized with the humorous overtone being lost.

noun:Kleber.tx: From Middle High German kleber, from Old High German *klebar (“sticky substance, resin”), from Proto-West Germanic *klibr (“resin, glue”). Cognate with Middle Low German klever, Middle Dutch clebber.

verb:klauen.tx: From earlier kläuen, from Middle High German kleuen, klæwen, from Old High German klawēn, chlawēn, klawjan, from Proto-Germanic *klawjaną. Later remodelled after and related to Klaue (“claw”), that is “to grab with one’s claws”. The sense “to steal” originated in West Central German and Low Franconian, and is supposed to have been spread among soldiers during World War I.
