noun:Koeffizient.tx: From New Latin coefficiēns/coëfficiēns, a substantivization of the present active participle of coefficiō formed by the mathematician François Viète.

verb:krähen.tx: From Middle High German kræ(je)n, from Old High German krāen, from Proto-West Germanic *krāan (“to crow, shout”).

noun:Kriegsrecht.tx: From Krieg (“war”) + -s- + Recht (“law”). Compare Swedish krigsrätt.

adj:koscher.tx: Borrowed from Yiddish כּשר (kosher), from Hebrew כָּשֵׁר (kašér).

noun:Kollaps.tx: 19th century, learned borrowing from Latin collāpsus.

noun:Konvoi.tx: 16th century, from Middle French convoi. Some uses as well as the pronunciation may have been influenced by cognate English convoy. Until the earlier 20th century it was often pronounced as in French.

verb:kapern.tx: Derived from Dutch kaper (“pirate”). The underlying Dutch verb is kapen.

noun:Kajak.tx: Borrowed in the 17th century from a descendant of Proto-Eskimo *qayaʀ, such as Greenlandic qajaq or Inuktitut ᖃᔭᖅ (qayaq). See English kayak for more.

noun:Katalog.tx: From Late Latin catalogus, from Ancient Greek κατάλογος (katálogos, “an enrollment, a register”), from καταλέγω (katalégō, “to recount, to tell at length”), from κατά (katá, “downwards, towards”) + λέγω (légō, “to gather, to pick up, to choose for oneself, to pick out, to count”).

noun:Kriegsdienstverweigerer.tx: From Krieg (“war (i.e., military, national, selective)”) + -s- (“genitival interfix”) + Dienst (“service”) + Verweigerer (“refuser”).

noun:Kadett.tx: Borrowed from French cadet. Compare Hunsrik Katett.

noun:Kufe.tx: From a dialectal variant, from Middle Low German kāk (“stake, rod”), Proto-Germanic *kōpǭ (“the prow of a sleigh”), ultimately related to the root of Kegel. Compare Old Norse kafl, kafli (“an elongated, round piece of wood”), Old Norse kefli (“a roll; scroll”), Middle Low German kavele (“cut wood used for lots”), dialectal German Kabel (“loose parts; odds and ends”).

verb:kappen.tx: 17th century, from Middle Low German kappen, from Middle Dutch cappen (“to chop”), perhaps a borrowing from Romansh and from Medieval Latin cappare (“to cut off”), from Vulgar Latin *cappo, from Latin capo (“castrated male chicken”). Compare Alemannic German (Alsatian) kchapfen (“to chop, mince”).

noun:Konnotation.tx: Borrowed from Medieval Latin connotātiō, from Latin connotō.

noun:Kappes.tx: From western German dialects including Central Franconian Kappes (“cabbage”). The meaning “nonsense” might be a loan translation of Kohl (etymology 2), the origins of which are quite unclear, however.

adj:kapriziös.tx: Borrowed from French capricieux. Doublet of capriccioso.

noun:Ketzer.tx: From Middle High German ketzer, from Old High German ketzer, kether, from Medieval Latin Catharī, from Medieval Greek Καθαροί (Katharoí), substantive form of Ancient Greek καθαρός (katharós, “pure”). Doublet of Katharer. See English Cathar.

verb:knirschen.tx: From Middle High German *knirsen (“gnashing”), of imitative origin (lautmalend). Cognate with Dutch knarsen (“to gnash, crash”).

verb:kichern.tx: Of imitative origin, or perhaps a fusion of Middle High German kitzern, kittern (“to giggle”), and German gickeln, gickern (“to giggle”).

verb:krabbeln.tx: From Middle Low German krabbelen (“to crawl”), an iterative form of krabben (“to scrape”). Compare Dutch krabbelen and krabben. Possibly derived from Krabbe (“crab”). A strong counterargument to this, however, is the cognate krappeln in Middle High German, which did not have the noun.

noun:Kartusche.tx: Borrowed from French cartouche, from Italian cartuccia. Doublet of Kartätsche.

noun:Kore.tx: Borrowed from Ancient Greek κόρη (kórē, “girl, maiden”).

adj:kräftig.tx: From Middle High German kreftic, kreftec, from Old High German kreftīg, from Proto-West Germanic *kraftīg, from Proto-Germanic *kraftugaz, equivalent to Kraft + -ig. Cognate with English crafty, Dutch krachtig.

noun:Killer.tx: Borrowed from English killer; analyzable as killen + -er.

noun:Kolumne.tx: 16th century, from Latin columna. Doublet of Kolonne (“column of troops etc.”).

noun:Kolumnist.tx: Since the 20th century. Kolumne + -ist, perhaps influenced by columnist.

verb:kentern.tx: Borrowed from German Low German kantern, kentern, derived from a cognate of Kante (“edge, brink”), originally in the general sense of "to put something on its side". Compare Dutch kenteren (probably borrowed from Low German) and Dutch kantelen.

noun:Kuhdorf.tx: Compound of Kuh (“cow's”, genitive singular) + Dorf (“village”).

noun:Kellnerin.tx: From Middle High German këlnærinne (“maid, servant, housekeeper”).

verb:koordinieren.tx: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin coordinare + -ieren.

noun:Konkurs.tx: From Latin concursus + creditorum (assembly of creditors)

noun:Kollekte.tx: 16th century, learned borrowing from Latin collecta.

noun:Krempe.tx: Borrowed from German Low German Kramp; a variant or derivative of Middle Low German krampe (“hook”), from Old Saxon krampo, from Proto-Germanic *krampō. Cognate with German Krampf, English cramp.

noun:Konditor.tx: Borrowed from Latin condītor, from condiō (“to season, make savory”).

noun:Karfreitag.tx: From Middle High German karvrītac, from kar ("lamentation; mourning"; from Old High German kara, chara) + vrītac (“Friday”). More at care, Friday.

noun:Kotau.tx: Ultimately from Chinese 叩頭 /叩头 (kòutóu), possibly through English kowtow.

noun:Käppi.tx: Originally an Alemannic German diminutive of Kappe.

verb:kreieren.tx: From French créer (from Latin creāre, from creō) + -ieren. Compare Hunsrik krieere.

noun:Klempner.tx: An originally Central and Low German word, derived from Middle Low German klampe (“clamp”).

noun:Ketchup.tx: Borrowed from English ketchup, from Malay kecap.

noun:Kap.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German kap, from Middle French cap. Compare Dutch kaap, English cape.

verb:knuddeln.tx: From Central German and German Low German [Term?] dialects; derived from a group of words meaning “knob, knot”. Compare Ripuarian Central Franconian Knöddel (“knot”), Middle Dutch knodde (“knob”). These words belong to the large group of stems related with Knoten (“knot”). The original sense of the verb is “to embrace tightly”; compare English canoodle in the same sense.

noun:Karabinerhaken.tx: Karabiner (“carbine”) + Haken (“hook”). Originally, in cavalry, a hook that could carry a carbine.

noun:Kerker.tx: From Middle High German kerker, kerkære, karkære, from Old High German karkāri, karkari, karkeri, from Proto-West Germanic *karkarī, ultimately from Latin carcer. Doublet of Karzer (“arrest cell, especially at a university”), a later borrowing of the same noun.

adj:klammheimlich.tx: Originally 19th c. student slang, from Latin clam (“secretly”) + heimlich (“secret”).

noun:Koben.tx: Middle High German kobe (“sty, shed”), from Old High German kubisi (“hut, tent”), from Proto-West Germanic *kobō, from Proto-Germanic *kubô (“shed, hut”).

noun:Kontrabass.tx: Borrowed from Italian contrabasso (da viola), from contra (“against”) + basso (“low”). Compare Medieval Latin contrabassus (“low male voice”).

noun:Köpfchen.tx: Kopf + -chen. The botanical sense is a semantic loan from Latin capitulum.

noun:Kantine.tx: Borrowed from French cantine, from Italian cantina.

noun:Kaiserschnitt.tx: Kaiser + Schnitt (“cut”), calque of Latin sectiō caesarēa.

noun:Kontingenz.tx: Borrowed from Late Latin contingentia, from contingō (“come into contact”).

noun:Kapaun.tx: From Middle High German kappūn, Old High German chappo; derived from Latin capo. Cognate with Dutch kapoen, English capon, French chapon, Ancient Greek κάπων (kápōn), Italian cappone.

noun:Kampfer.tx: From Middle High German kampfer, from Medieval Latin camphora, nasalized byform of cafora, from Arabic كَافُور (kāfūr), from an Austronesian language (cf. Malay kapur).

verb:kümmern.tx: From Middle High German kumbern, derived from the noun kumber, probably from Old French *combre (“obstruction, barrier”), itself probably from Gaulish. See Kummer for more. Cognate with Hunsrik kimmre, Luxembourgish këmmeren and Dutch kommer.

noun:Kiebitz.tx: From Middle High German *kibitz, a Central German byform of gībitz(e), whence Bavarian Geibitz. Further cognate with Middle Low German kī̆vit, kī̆wit. All ultimately onomatopoeic.

verb:kieken.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German kîken, from Old Saxon kīkan, from Proto-West Germanic *kīkan. The verb is strong in Low German, but treated as weak in standard German. Cognate with Dutch kijken. Compare also German gucken, kucken, which need not be originally related, but has probably been influenced by kieken.

verb:klicken.tx: 16th century, from Middle High German *klicken, attested in zerklicken (“to break an eggshell”). Either cognate with or analogous to Dutch klikken (15th c.), English click (16th c.), French cliquer (14th c.). All ultimately imitative. The computing sense is a semantic loan from English.

noun:Kamille.tx: Middle High German gamille, Medieval Latin camomilla.

noun:Kondor.tx: From Spanish cóndor, from Quechua kuntur.

verb:kuscheln.tx: Iterative form of kuschen (“to lie down”) + -eln, from French se coucher. The form is late in standard usage (around 1900), but widespread and significantly older in dialects.

verb:kränken.tx: From Middle High German krenken (“to make ill”), from kranc (“ill”), ultimately from the root of krank (“ill”). Cognate with Dutch krenken and Luxembourgish kränken.

noun:Kür.tx: From Middle High German küre, Old High German kuri, from Proto-West Germanic *kuʀi.

noun:Klammeraffe.tx: From klammern (“to cling”) + Affe (“monkey”). In the informal sense “stapler”, perhaps reanalysed as Klammer (“staple”) + Affe.

noun:Kukuruz.tx: Attested from 1697. From Serbo-Croatian kukuruz or Romanian cucuruz (see there for further etymology). Compare Russian кукуруза (kukuruza), Hungarian kukorica, Slovene koruza, Polish kukurydza, etc.

noun:Kanten.tx: From Middle Dutch cant, cante (“edge, rim, piece of bread”), adopted from Dutch settlers in East Elbia since the 12th century. Compare synonymous German Kante.

noun:Kar.tx: From Middle High German kar, from Old High German char (“bowl; dish”), from Proto-Germanic *kazą (“vessel; container”).

noun:Kongolese.tx: From Kongo + -ese with an additional l.

noun:Kibbuz.tx: Borrowed from Hebrew קַבְּצָן (kibúts, “gathering, clustering”), קבוץ (kibúts), קיבוץ (kibúts).

noun:Kombüse.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German kabūse, later influenced by early modern Dutch combuys (now spelt kombuis). The further origin of this word is unsettled.

verb:klappern.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German klapperen, an iterative form of klappen. Compare Dutch klapperen.

verb:kramen.tx: From Middle High German krāmen, equivalent to Kram (“shop, stall, booth”) + -en.

noun:Katafalk.tx: Borrowed from French catafalque, from Italian catafalco, from Vulgar Latin *catafalicum. Doublet of Schafott.

noun:Kimber.tx: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek Κίμβρος (Kímbros). Introduced to distinguish from Zimber (“speaker of a Bavarian variety in Italy”).

noun:Kaff.tx: 19th century, from Romani gav (“village”), from Sanskrit ग्राम (grāma, “village”). Probably influenced by Rotwelsch kefar, from Hebrew כְּפָר (kfar, “village”); perhaps also by etymology 2 in the sense of “something worthless”. The now common plural in -er probably after Dörfer.

noun:Krätze.tx: From Late Middle High German kretz, kratz (15th c.). Derived from kratzen (“to scratch”).

noun:Kristallnacht.tx: From Kristall (“crystal”) + Nacht (“night”), alluding to the crystals of broken glass from the destroyed shop and synagogue windows.

adj:konservativ.tx: Borrowed from English conservative in the 1830s, from Medieval Latin conservatīvus, from cōnservāre (“preserve, conserve”) + -īvus.

noun:Kadi.tx: First attested in the 16th century. From Arabic قَاضِي (qāḍī), possibly through a French intermediate French cadi.

noun:Kläger.tx: Inherited from Middle High German kleger, klager, from Old High German klagāri. Equivalent to Klage or klagen + -er.

noun:Kapo.tx: Clipping of Kaporal (Upper German), from Italian caporale (“corporal”), from Italian capo, from Vulgar Latin capus, from Latin caput. There is some uncertainty about the etymology of the sense "prisoner functionary". Pfeifer connects it to the same etymology as above, however Duden claims an origin in French caporal. adv:keineswegs.tx: Univerbation of keines + Wegs, adverbial genitive of kein Weg.

verb:klönen.tx: Borrowed from German Low German *klönen (“to sound, speak in a rambling manner”), likely of imitative origin (lautmalend).

verb:knallen.tx: From Knall. Compare Middle High German knellen (“to bang”). Compare Dutch knallen, Swedish knulla.

noun:Küster.tx: From Middle High German kuster, custer, from Old High German kustor, kostor, from Proto-West Germanic *kustārī.

noun:Knäckebrot.tx: Partial calque of Swedish knäckebröd. The first component is unaltered from Swedish knäcka (“to crack, snap”). German-speakers commonly analyse it as knacken + Brot, which is ultimately both semantically and etymologically correct.

verb:kapieren.tx: Borrowed from Latin capere (“to seize, catch; to understand”), possibly with influence from Italian capire (“to understand”). First used in 17th-century grammar-school slang. Doublet of heben and hieven; cognate with English capture.

noun:Karbunkel.tx: 16th century, from Latin carbunculus. Doublet of Karfunkel.

noun:Klabusterbeere.tx: From klabustern (“to smear, to soil”) + Beere (“berry”).

verb:kritzeln.tx: Diminutive of Middle High German kritzen, from Old High German krizzōn (“to scratch”), probably from the root of modern kratzen (“to scratch”).

verb:krachen.tx: From Middle High German krachen, from Old High German krahhōn, from Proto-West Germanic *krakōn. Cognate with Bavarian kråchn, kråcha, Dutch kraken, Old English cracian and English crack.

noun:Kresse.tx: From Middle High German kresse, from Old High German kressa, from Proto-West Germanic *krassjā. Cognates include English cress.

verb:kehren.tx: From Middle High German keren, kern, from Old High German kerian, kerien, from Proto-Germanic *karjaną.

adj:kirre.tx: From Middle High German kirre (“docile”), unrounding of kürre, from Old High German *quirri, *querri, from Proto-Germanic *kwerruz (“calm”). Cognate with Danish kvær, Swedish kvar, Gothic 𐌵𐌰𐌹𐍂𐍂𐌿𐍃 (qairrus). The semantic development from “docile” to “confused” may have occurred in the context of flirting (kirre machen originally “make weak, amenable”, now usually understood as “make unable to …

verb:kallen.tx: From Middle High German kallen, Old High German kallōn, from Proto-West Germanic *kalʀōn, from Proto-Germanic *kalzōną. Cognate with Dutch kallen, English call.

noun:Kalmus.tx: Inherited from Middle High German kalmus, from Latin calamus.

adj:kindlich.tx: From Middle High German [Term?], from Old High German [Term?]; Kind (“child”) + -lich.

verb:kennenlernen.tx: kennen (“to be acquainted with”) + lernen (“to learn”).

noun:Kleinod.tx: From Middle High German kleinōt, kleinœte, kleinœde, from Old High German *kleinōti, from Proto-West Germanic *klainōdī (“jewel, trinket”).

noun:Kalifat.tx: Borrowed from Medieval Latin calīphātus. By surface analysis, Kalif + -at.

noun:Klerus.tx: Borrowed from Latin clērus, from Ancient Greek κλῆρος (klêros).

noun:Kartei.tx: Karte + -ei, 19th century, in analogy to words like Bücherei.

noun:Kommissar.tx: Ultimately from Latin commissarius, from commissus, past participle of committō (“to commit, entrust to”).

noun:Kram.tx: From Middle High German krām (“merchant tent; wares”), from Old High German krām (“merchant tent; tent cloth”), probably ultimately borrowed from Slavic, such as Old Church Slavonic грамъ (gramŭ, “pub, inn”) or чрѣмъ (črěmŭ, “tent”). The semantic development is “tent cloth” → “merchant tent” → “shop” → “wares” → “stuff”. Cognate with Dutch kraam (“booth, stall”) and Yiddish קראָם (krom, “shop”). More at crame.

adj:krass.tx: 18th century, from Latin crassus. See English crass for more.

noun:Kachelofen.tx: From Middle High German kacheloven. Equivalent to Kachel + Ofen.

verb:knistern.tx: From Middle Low German knisteren, gnisteren. Also a Central German and Dutch word; compare Middle Dutch gnisteren (but modern Dutch knisteren probably from German). Eventually onomatopoeic.

noun:Kautschuk.tx: Borrowed from French caoutchouc, from Spanish caucho, from Quechua kawchu.

noun:Kosmopolit.tx: From Ancient Greek κοσμοπολίτης (kosmopolítēs, “citizen of the world”) (κόσμος (kósmos, “world”) + πολίτης (polítēs, “citizen”)).

noun:Kontra.tx: Ultimatively from Latin contra. Doublet of Konter.

noun:Kutter.tx: Borrowed from English cutter, from to cut.

noun:Konterfei.tx: Middle High German kunterfeit, from Old French contrefait, Medieval Latin contrafacere.

noun:Kaisersemmel.tx: May be Kaiser (“emperor”) + Semmel (“roll”). Kayser may also be a baker's surname. More at Wikipedia.

noun:Konsole.tx: Borrowed from French console and English console.

verb:küren.tx: Seemingly derived from Kür. Possibly conflated with Old High German korōn, from Proto-West Germanic *koʀōn, which does not, however, seem to have attested continuations in Middle High German. Originally a weak verb, the strong past forms kor, gekoren came from the related verb kiesen. Compare Middle Low German kören (whence German kören), Dutch keuren, and Middle English curen (“to select”).

verb:konsumieren.tx: From Latin cōnsūmere, from con- + sūmere, equivalent to Konsum + -ieren.

verb:kontakten.tx: From English contact + -en. Doublet of kontaktieren.

noun:Katakana.tx: From Japanese 片(かた)仮(か)名(な) (katakana).

noun:Kerbel.tx: From Middle High German kervel, from Old High German kervil, from Latin caerefolium, chaerephyllum, from Ancient Greek χαιρέφυλλον (khairéphullon).

adj:kolonial.tx: From French colonial. By surface analysis, Kolonie + -al.

noun:Karawanserei.tx: 17th century, from Ottoman Turkish كاروانسَرای (karvanseray), كَروانسَرای (kervanseray), from Persian کاروانسرای (kârvânsarây), from کاروان (kârvân, “caravan”) + سرای (sarây, “courtyard, dwelling, palace”). Reanalysed as Karawane + -s- + -erei, whence the feminine gender. Compare the English variant caravansary.

verb:knutschen.tx: From East Central German and eastern German Low German [Term?]. Originally the same word as knautschen (“to squeeze”), which see for more.

noun:Kamp.tx: From Middle Low German kamp, from Old Saxon kamp, from Proto-West Germanic *kamp, from Latin campus. Thus originally the same word as Kampf (“fight”).

adj:konzeptuell.tx: From English conceptual, with assimilation to the nativized suffix -ell. By surface analysis, Konzept + -uell.

verb:konkurrieren.tx: From Latin concurrō (“run with”) + -ieren. Cognate with English concur.

verb:kauern.tx: Borrowed from Low German, eventually from Middle Low German kūren (“to lurk”, originally "to crouch, bend, sit hunched over"), whence also English cower, according to Pokorny, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gew- (“to curve, bend”), see also Proto-Germanic *kuddô (“shell, pod”). Used in standard German since the 18th century, either directly from German Low German (then with an artificial …

verb:konvertieren.tx: From French convertir, from Latin converto.

noun:Ketzerei.tx: From Middle High German ketzerīe. By surface analysis, Ketzer + -ei. Cognate with Low German Ketterie, Ketteree (“heresy”).

noun:Kaisertum.tx: From Middle High German keisertuom borrowed from Old High German cheisertuom. Equivalent to Kaiser + -tum.

adj:kaiserlich.tx: Kaiser + -lich or Middle High German keiserlich

noun:Kaschemme.tx: From Romani katšima, eventually from Proto-Slavic *kъrčьma. Doublet of regional Kretscham.

adj:kauderwelsch.tx: From earlier kuderwelsch since the first part of the 16th century. By surface analysis, Kauder + welsch, in reference to the variety of Romansh spoken in the Swiss town of Kauder (Chur).

noun:Kontor.tx: Since 16th century, borrowed from Middle Low German kontôr, kuntôr, kumptôr (“commercial branch; writing room; counting desk”), from Middle Dutch contoor, comptoir (modern kantoor), from Middle French contoir, comptoer, from compter (“to count”) + -oir. See English counter for more.

noun:Kauffrau.tx: Constructed in analogy to German Kaufmann.

verb:kiesen.tx: From Middle High German kiesen, from Old High German kiosan, from Proto-West Germanic *keusan, from Proto-Germanic *keusaną (“to choose”). Cognate with Low German kesen, Dutch kiezen, English choose, Danish kyse, Icelandic kjósa, Gothic 𐌺𐌹𐌿𐍃𐌰𐌽 (kiusan).

verb:knittern.tx: Originally of imitative origin (lautmalend), similar to German knattern (“rattling”), with which it shares an ablaut relationship.

noun:Kummerbund.tx: Borrowed from English cummerbund, from Hindustani کمر بند / कमरबंद (kamarband), from Classical Persian کمربند (kamarband), derived from کمر (kamar, “waist”) + بند (band, “band”). The English -u- (instead of more etymological -a-) is a pronunciation spelling representing Hindi [ɐ]. In German, in turn, this -u- was given a spelling pronunciation, leading to [ʊ] as well as a remotivation as Kummer …

verb:kollern.tx: Either onomatopoeic or denominal from Koller ascribing an angry disposition to the creature that utters such sounds.

verb:kokeln.tx: North and East Central German variant of gaukeln.

noun:Konzil.tx: From Middle High German concili, concilje (13th c.), from Latin concilium.

noun:Kernwaffe.tx: Kern + Waffe. Compare Russian я́дерное ору́жие (jádernoje orúžije), English nuclear weapon.

verb:koppeln.tx: Inherited from Middle High German koppeln, kuppeln, kupelen (“to bind (to a paddock, chiefly dogs); to pinion”), a hunting jargon term borrowed from Old French copler, coupler. Doublet of kuppeln.

noun:Kurzweil.tx: From Middle High German kurzewile, kurzwile (“short while; reduction of time”). For more, see "kurz", "Weile". Cognate with Dutch kortwijl and kortswijl.

noun:Kick.tx: Borrowed from English kick. In the football sense, partly a backformation from kicken (“to kick, to play football”).

verb:kugeln.tx: From Middle High German kugelen. Equivalent to Kugel (“ball”) + -en.

verb:konzipieren.tx: From Late Middle High German concipieren, from Latin concipiō (“I conceive”).

noun:Kopp.tx: From Central and Low German dialects, from northern Middle High German and Middle Low German kop. Compare Appel, kloppen, Knopp, and several other such forms that are usual in colloquial Standard German.

noun:Knubbel.tx: A Central German and German Low German word, derived from Middle Low German knobbe (whence also English knob); see Knopf (“button”). Cognate with Dutch knobbel.

verb:kräftigen.tx: Denominal verb of kräftig, already Middle High German kreftigen, Old High German chreftigôn.

noun:Katarrh.tx: Borrowed from Latin catarrhus, from Ancient Greek κατάρροος (katárrhoos).

noun:Konklave.tx: Early 15th century, borrowed from Latin conclāve n.

verb:kleiden.tx: From Middle High German kleiden, from Old High German [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *klaiþōną (“to clothe”). Cognate to English clothe.

verb:klammern.tx: From Middle High German klammern, klammeren, from Old High German *klammarōn, from Proto-Germanic *klammarōną, from Proto-Indo-European *glem-, from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“to amass, ball up”). Related to Middle High German klemberen (“to stick together, cling”).

noun:Kabloona.tx: Via English kabloona, from Eastern Canadian Inuktitut [Term?] or Greenlandic [Term?], or a combination of the two; see kabloona for more.

noun:Köpper.tx: From Kopp, the Low and Central German form of standard Kopf ("head").

noun:Krapp.tx: Borrowed from Middle Dutch crappe, from Proto-Germanic *krappô (“hook”), a reference to the plant’s hook-shaped thorns. Doublet of Krapfen.

noun:Klient.tx: Borrowed from Latin cliēns; cognate with Hunsrik Klïent. Doublet of Client (“client (computing)”).

verb:kabbeln.tx: Borrowed from German Low German [Term?], from Middle Low German kabbelen. Probably related to Kiefer (“jaw”) and originally meaning “to move one’s jaws (in order to speak or bite)”. Cognate with Dutch kabbelen (“to babble”).

verb:künden.tx: Corresponding to kund + -en. From Middle High German künden, from Old High German kunden, from Proto-West Germanic *kunþijan (“to make known”), from Proto-Germanic *kunþijaną (“to make known”). Cognate with Scottish dialectal English kithe.

noun:Kamelle.tx: Ripuarian, a corruption of Karamelle (“caramel sweets”).

noun:Kabale.tx: Borrowed from French cabale, from Hebrew קַבָּלָה.

noun:Klamotte.tx: First attested ca. 1900 in Berlin, whence it spread. Further origin uncertain.

verb:korrelieren.tx: Back-formation from Korrelation, from Medieval Latin correlātiō, suffixed with -ieren.

verb:kullern.tx: Borrowed from German Low German and Central German dialects. Derived from a contracted form of Kugel (“ball”).

verb:kranken.tx: Inherited from Middle High German kranken (“to be sick”), equivalent to krank + -en.

verb:korrodieren.tx: Borrowed from French corroder, from Latin corrodere (“to gnaw”).

noun:Koppel.tx: Borrowed from Old French cople, couple, from Latin copula.

noun:Kühnheit.tx: From kühn + -heit. Cognate to Dutch koenheid.

noun:Kriminalität.tx: From French criminalité (“crime, criminality”), equivalent to kriminal + -ität.

adv:kurzerhand.tx: Univerbation of kurzer + Hand, calque of Latin brevī manū.

noun:Kassa.tx: Borrowed from Italian cassa (“case, crate”), from Latin capsa (“box”).

noun:Kondition.tx: Borrowed from Medieval Latin conditiō, from Latin condiciō.

noun:Kundschaft.tx: From Middle High German kuntschaft; by surface analysis, Kunde + -schaft.

verb:kurieren.tx: From Latin curō + -ieren; equivalent to Kur + -ieren.

noun:Kodex.tx: Borrowed from Latin cōdex. Doublet of Code.

verb:kraulen.tx: Iterative of now unused krauen, from Middle High German krouwen, from Old High German krouwōn, krouwen, from Proto-Germanic *krawwōną. Compare Dutch krauwen. Related to Proto-Germanic *krawa- (“claw”), from Proto-Indo-European *gar-, *ger- (“to tie, bind together”), whence probably also Proto-Germanic *krumô (“fragment”), Latin grypus (“hooknose”), gry (“dirt under the fingernails”).

adj:knusprig.tx: Derived in the 19th century from knuspern (“to nibble audibly, to crunch”), borrowed around 1800 from German Low German knuspern. Apparently onomatopoeic in origin.

verb:knien.tx: Inherited from Middle High German kniewen, from Old High German gikniuwen, kniuwen. By surface analysis, Knie + -en.

verb:kränkeln.tx: From kranken (“to be sick”) + -eln (iterative suffix), since the 17th century.

verb:krächzen.tx: From late Middle High German krachitzen, ultimately from the root of krachen (“to crunch”).

noun:Kuhle.tx: A Central and Low German word from Middle Low German [Term?] and northern Middle High German kūle, ultimately from the root of Keule (“club”). The regular High German development is seen in older Kaule, the modern form was introduced via German Low German. Cognate to Dutch kuil, Luxembourgish Kaul.

verb:klarmachen.tx: From klar + machen, literally “to make clear”.

adj:kundig.tx: From Middle High German kündec, kündic, from Old High German kundīg, from Proto-West Germanic *kunþīg, from Proto-Germanic *kunþīgaz, from Proto-Germanic *kunþaz, originally the past participle of *kunnaną, whose modern form is können. Equivalent to kund + -ig.

noun:Kuppe.tx: From Middle High German kupfe, from Old High German kupfa (“cap, bonnet”), probably from Late Latin cuppa (“cup”). The modern consonantism is Central and Low German; compare Middle Low German koppe. Cognate with Dutch kop (“cup; head”), English cup. Related also with Kopf (“head”).

noun:Kuppel.tx: Borrowed from Italian cupola, from Latin cupula (“little tub”); from cupa, cuppa (“cup”); named for its resemblance to a cup turned over. Doublet of Kübel.

phrase:k. u. k..tx: Abbreviation of kaiserlich und königlich (Imperial and Royal).

noun:Krampus.tx: Unclear, but nigh-certainly Germanic. Possibly related to Krampen (“axe, pickaxe”), but see notes in entry at Etymonline.

noun:Kolkrabe.tx: Probably from an onomatopoeic kolk- + Rabe.

noun:Klicker.tx: An onomatopoetic word already attested in Middle High German klucker. Another variant of the same is Dutch knikker.

noun:Kanzel.tx: From Middle High German kanzel, Old High German cancella (“the place set apart for the priests”); derived from Late Latin cancellus (“grating”). Cognate with English chancel.

noun:Kaiman.tx: From Spanish caimán or Portuguese caimão, from Kari'na acayouman.

verb:kosen.tx: From Middle High German kōsen, from Old High German kōson, ultimately borrowed from Latin causa.

noun:Kehrseite.tx: From kehren + Seite, borrowed from, or influenced by, Dutch keerzijde.

adj:kölnisch.tx: Köln + -isch; Middle High German kölnisch (variae lectiones: kolnsch, köllisch, kolsch)

verb:konsultieren.tx: Since the 18th century, replacing the older konsulieren. Both are learned borrowing from Latin cōnsulere. Compare also the earlier-borrowed Konsultation.

noun:Kabuff.tx: Probably derived from Middle Low German kabūse (“shed”) (compare Kombüse) through conflation with another word, which may either Dutch kombof (“hovel”) or one from the root of German Koben (“stable, shed”). Commonly associated with Rotwelsch, and possibly spread by it.

noun:Kämpe.tx: Modern (18th century) borrowing from Middle Low German kempe, from Old Saxon kempio; see Kampf. The revived word existed also in an Upper German form: Middle High German kempfe, from Old High German kempho, which is preserved as a surname in the form German Kempf.

noun:Klause.tx: From Middle High German klūse, from Old High German klūsa, from Proto-West Germanic *klūsā.

verb:kasteien.tx: From Middle Low German and northern Middle High German kastīen, kastīgen, variant of kestigen, from Old High German kestigōn (“to castigate”), from Proto-West Germanic *kastīgōn. The northern form was spread by Luther.

verb:keifen.tx: From Middle High German kīben, from Old High German *kīban, from Proto-West Germanic *kīban (“to quarrel”). The modern form with a fricative is of Low and West Central German origin; compare Middle Low German kīven. The original plosive is preserved in the Upper German iterative form kibbeln and keppeln, in Bavarian keppln, and in Alemannic German kebbeln. Cognate with Dutch kijven.

noun:Kescher.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German kesser. A relation with English catch, catcher is possible, though direct borrowing (as assumed by Kluge, edition 24) seems doubtful.

noun:Kimme.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German kimme (“edge; horizon”). Doublet of Kimm. Cognate with Dutch kim (“horizon”).

noun:Kirchhof.tx: From Middle High German kirchhof (“land around a church”). Analyzable as Kirche (“church”) + Hof (“yard”). The semantic development is determined by Middle Low German kerkhof, which came to mean “graveyard” because graveyards have traditionally tended to be established around churches. Compare the same in Dutch kerkhof (“graveyard”).

noun:Kittchen.tx: From a criminal slang word (Rotwelsch) for “house”, which is derived from Middle Low German kōte, whence also German Kate (“hut”). The form Kittchen, though formally a diminutive, is likely to be explained by conflation with unrelated Middle High German kīche (“jail”). Unrelated to English kitchen.

noun:Knallfolie.tx: knallen (“to pop”) + Folie (“wrap”). From the popping sound that bubble wrap makes if it is squeezed.

verb:klarkommen.tx: klar (“clear”) + kommen (“to come”). Not to be confused with klaarkomen in Dutch.

noun:Kladde.tx: Borrowed from German Low German Kladde (“spot, stain”), derived from Middle Low German kladderen (“to soil”). Compare Dutch klad. The standard German sense is probably shortened from a compound, such as attested kladdebuch, that is "book for careless notes".

noun:Klacks.tx: A German Low German [Term?] and Central German derivative in -s from the verb klacken (“to clack”).

noun:Klei.tx: 16th c., borrowed from Middle Low German klei, from Old Saxon *klēi, from Proto-West Germanic *klaij.

noun:Kleister.tx: From northern Middle High German klīster, an originally Central German word, possibly from Old High German *klīstar, from Proto-West Germanic *klīstr, from Proto-Germanic *klīstrą (“paste, goo”), ultimately from the root of Klei (“clay”). Cognate with German Low German Kliester, Dutch klijster, Saterland Frisian Klíester, Scots cleester. Related also to English clay. Compare also Middle High …

noun:Kliff.tx: 20th-century borrowing from German Low German Klipp, from Middle Low German klif, from Old Saxon klif, from Proto-West Germanic *klib, from Proto-Germanic *klibą. Cognate with Dutch klif, English cliff.

noun:Klinker.tx: Borrowed from Dutch klinker, which pertains to the cognate of German klingen (“to sound”), from the clear sound the brick makes when struck against.

noun:Klops.tx: From German Low German, probably borrowed from Swedish kalops (“stewed meat”), from Old Swedish kollops (“slices of beef stew”), ultimately related to klopfen (“to beat”). Cognate to English collop (“slice of meat, bacon, rasher”).

noun:Klöten.tx: Plural of German Low German Kloot, from Middle Low German klôt, from Old Saxon *klōt, from Proto-Germanic *klautaz (“ball”). Cognate with High German Kloß (“dumpling”) and Dutch kloot, of which the latter may have the same anatomic sense.

verb:knipsen.tx: From the now dated noun Knips (“flip; dab”), itself derived with the northern suffix -s from the verb Middle Low German knippen (“to flip; to slap; to wink”). Compare Dutch knippen. This verb may plausibly be thought to be derived from Middle Low German knīpen (“to squeeze”) (see kneifen), but onomatopoeia has certainly played a role in the development of this root.

verb:knuffen.tx: Borrowed from German Low German, of imitative origin (lautmalend). Or, of a class of kn- words also containing Knopf (“knob, button”). Compare Dutch knuffelen (“to cuddle”).

verb:knuspern.tx: Borrowed from German Low German, of imitative origin. May be related to Norwegian Nynorsk knuspe (“break off a small piece”).

noun:Knust.tx: Borrowed from Low German Knuust, from Middle Low German knūst. Compare Dutch knoest and knuist. Possibly from Proto-Indo-European *ǵénus (“cheek, jaw, chin”) and its synonymous derivative *ǵn̥h₂dʰ(h₁)-. Then cognate with Latvian zods (“chin, sharp edge”), Lithuanian žándas (“cheek”) and Ancient Greek γνάθος (gnáthos, “jaw, point, edge”). The same etymology should apply to the dialectal variants …

verb:krakeelen.tx: Via Middle Low German krakēlen from early modern Dutch krakelen (“to quarrel loudly”). Further origin unknown. Most probably derived from Middle Dutch kreel, which is borrowed from Middle French querelle. Other (secondary?) influences may include Dutch kraken (“to crack”) and keel (“throat”).

verb:kribbeln.tx: From Middle High German kribeln (“to tickle”). The modern form is based more on Low German and Central German dialects, belonging to krabbeln (“to crawl; to tickle”).

noun:Kuddelmuddel.tx: Borrowed from German Low German Kuddelmuddel. The word originally meant "dirty linen" and is derived from the verb koddeln (“to wash clothes superficially”). The rhyming part might be based on a cognate of German Modder (“mud”), a Dutch form of which also led to English muddle.

noun:Kanzlei.tx: From Middle High German kanzelie, itself borrowed from Late Latin cancellarius (“secretary, porter”).

verb:klirren.tx: From East Central German and of imitative origin.

noun:Klassenzimmer.tx: From Klasse (“class”) + -n- + Zimmer (“room”). The use of the word Zimmer is slightly unusual in this compound because it is chiefly used for private rooms.

noun:Karlchen.tx: From Karl + -chen. Cognate to English Charlie.

noun:Kontur.tx: 18th century, borrowed from French contour m. Feminine gender by (etymologically unfounded) analogy with words in -tur (Latin -tura).

noun:Konstitution.tx: From Middle High German constitucion, borrowed from Latin cōnstitūtio.

verb:kommandieren.tx: From French commander + -ieren, from Latin commandare.

noun:Knutschfleck.tx: knutschen (“to kiss passionately, make out”) + Fleck (“spot”)

noun:Klappstuhl.tx: From klappen (“to fold”) + Stuhl (“chair”); cognate with Plautdietsch Klaupstool.

noun:Klebeband.tx: From kleben (“to stick, to glue”) + Band (“tape”).

noun:Karwoche.tx: From Middle High German karwoche (literally “mourning week”).

adj:keusch.tx: From Middle High German kiusch, from Old High German chūski, from Proto-West Germanic *kūskī (“chaste”).

noun:Kuguar.tx: From French couguar, from Brazilian Portuguese suçuarana, from Old Tupi sûasuarana.

adj:knusper.tx: Probably a variation of earlier knusprig in the same sense. Attested by the 1980s.

noun:Kreuzzeichen.tx: Kreuz (“cross”) + Zeichen (“sign”). Calque of Latin signum crucis.

noun:Kaki.tx: Learned borrowing from Japanese 柿(かき) (kaki).

noun:Kanon.tx: From Latin canōn, from Ancient Greek κανών (kanṓn, “measuring rod, standard”).

noun:Kötter.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German [Term?]. Derived from the noun kotte, kōte (“hut, cottage”), whence German Kate (“hut”). Compare English cotter.

noun:Köttel.tx: From Middle Low German kötel. Also a Low and Central Franconian word. Cognate with Dutch keutel. Unrelated to German Kot (“feces”); instead, probably derived from the noun at hand in Dutch koot (“little bone”), thus originally “something hard”. Compare German Köte (“the heelbone of a horse; fetlock”).

noun:Kehricht.tx: From kehren + -ich + -t (an element of no semantic content appearing often after -ig / -ich in Early New High German).

noun:Keuschheit.tx: From Middle High German kiuscheit. Analyzable as keusch + -heit.

noun:Kiepe.tx: 15th century, from Middle Low German kīpe. Cognate with dialectal Dutch kiep, English kipe (“basket used for catching fish”).

noun:Kiez.tx: Unknown, 13th c. Perhaps from a Slavic language, compare Slovak chyža (“hut”), from Proto-Slavic *xyža. Compare German Haus.

noun:Kokos.tx: Borrowed from Portuguese cocos, plural of coco (literally “grinning face”), probably due to the three holes in the shell resembling a human face.

adj:kleingläubig.tx: From klein (“small, little”) + gläubig (“believing, faithful”), a calque of Ancient Greek ὀλιγόπιστος (oligópistos).

verb:köcheln.tx: From kochen (“to boil”) + -eln (diminutive and frequentative suffix).

noun:Kunkel.tx: From Middle High German kunkel, from Medieval Latin conucla, conucula, colucula, corrupted from Latin colus (“distaff”).

noun:Koller.tx: From Middle High German kolre, from Old High German koloro, from Medieval Latin cholera (“outburst of anger”), from Latin cholera (“bile, anger”). Doublet of Cholera. Cognate with English choler.

noun:Kantor.tx: 15th century, learned borrowing from Latin cantor.

noun:Kimm.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German kimme (“edge; horizon”). Doublet of Kimme. Cognate with Dutch kim (“horizon”).

noun:Kober.tx: Middle High German kober, probably variant to the present Koben.

noun:Klepper.tx: Borrowed from Low German, probably kleppen (“to strike rapidly, ring with a sharp sound”) (referring to bells on the harness), probably ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *klappōn (“to strike, clap”).

noun:Kindel.tx: Inherited from Middle High German kindel, from Old High German chindili. By surface analysis, Kind + -el.

adj:kiebig.tx: Borrowed from German Low German, same as High German keibig from keiben, keifen.

adj:klatschnass.tx: From klatschen + nass. Compare Dutch kletsnat.

adj:knifflig.tx: From regional kniffeln (“to puzzle, put together intricately”) + -ig in the 19th century, though commonly perceived as derived from Kniff (“trick”) instead.

adj:knülle.tx: 19th century, of uncertain origin. Possibly from knollig, knöllig (“lumpy, chunky”, obsolete also “massive”), for which there are early attestations in the context of excessive drinking; further from Knolle (“lump, tuber”). Alternatively from knüllen (“to scrunch, crumple”, obsolete also “to beat, bump, fuck”).

adj:konsterniert.tx: Past participle of obsolete konsternieren, from French consterner, from Latin cōnsternāre, cōnsternō (“to alarm”).

adj:kunterbunt.tx: From dialectal contrabund, from Kontrapunkt (“counterpoint”) via folk etymology.

adj:kymrisch.tx: Borrowed from Welsh Cymr- as in Cymro (“Welsh person”), Cymry (“Welsh people”), Cymru (“Wales”), Cymraeg (“Welsh [of the language]”), Cymreig (“Welsh [of the culture]”) with the adjective suffix -isch.

adj:kündbar.tx: Historically from künden + -bar, where künden is used in the archaic/regional sense of “to terminate, resign, dismiss”, for which otherwise kündigen. Synchronically also analysable as a contraction of underlying *kündigbar; compare a similar case in unleugbar for *unleugenbar, from leugnen.

noun:Kosak.tx: From Old East Slavic козакъ (kozakŭ), through older Russian козак (kozak) and/or Polish kozak. See English Cossack for more.

noun:Knittel.tx: From Middle High German knüttel, from Old High German chnutil, ultimately from the root of Knoten (“knot”).

noun:Kanüle.tx: Borrowed from French canule, from Latin cannula.

noun:Kretschmer.tx: From Proto-Slavic *kъrčьmařь from *kъrčьma + *-ařь, or an analogous form in an early western daughter language of Proto-Slavic.

noun:Karner.tx: Middle High German, from Medieval Latin carnārium.

noun:Kulak.tx: Borrowed from Russian кула́к (kulák, “wealthy farmer”, literally “fist”). The Russian word probably comes from Turkic *kulak, with the same meaning, from *kul (“hand”).

noun:Kipper.tx: From kippen (“to tip over, to dump”) + -er.

noun:Kumpf.tx: From Middle High German kumpf, kumph (also kump, komp), from Old High German *kumpf, *kump, *kumb, from Proto-Germanic *kumbaz.

noun:Kotter.tx: Same as the Northern Kate (“hut”), English cot.

noun:Knack.tx: From Middle High German knacke, from Middle High German knacken (“to crack, crackle”).

noun:Knigge.tx: Named after German writer Adolph Freiherr Knigge (1752–1796).

noun:Klemmer.tx: Short form of Nasenklemmer (“nose-clamp”), a calque of French pince-nez.

intj:Ker.tx: Clipping of Kerl (“guy”), hence also the capitalisation.

intj:klaro.tx: Borrowed from Spanish claro. Küpper dates it to ca. 1975, though glossing it as "understandably". Doublet of klar.

noun:Kübel.tx: From Middle High German kübel, from Old High German kubilo, a vinicultural loan from Latin cūpula. Doublet of Kuppel.

noun:Kartenspieler.tx: From Karte (“card”) + Spieler (“player”) or Kartenspiel (“card game”) + -er (“-er”).

noun:Korpus.tx: Borrowed from Latin corpus (“body”) with Germanized spelling but retention of the Latin gender and plural. Doublet of Körper and Korps.

verb:killern.tx: Probably from Low German killern, apparently iterative of *killen, kiddeln, from Middle Low German kittelen, kētelen, from Old Saxon kitilōn, from Proto-Germanic *kitilōną. For the phonetic development compare especially Danish kilde, kildre, Norwegian kile. Also cognate with German kitzeln, Dutch kietelen, English kittle.

noun:Kreation.tx: In part directly from Latin creātiō, in part through French création. By surface analysis, kreieren + -ation.

verb:kuppeln.tx: Inherited from Middle High German koppeln, kuppeln, kupelen (“to bind (to a paddock, chiefly dogs); to pinion”), a hunting jargon term borrowed from Old French copler, coupler. Doublet of koppeln.

noun:Kleeblatt.tx: From Middle High German klēblat, from Old High German klēblat, equivalent to Klee (“clover”) + Blatt (“leaf”).

noun:Kolleg.tx: Borrowed from Latin collēgium. Doublet of Kollegium and College.

noun:Kollateralschaden.tx: kollateral (“collateral”) + Schaden (“damage”); calque of English collateral damage.

noun:Käsehobel.tx: Käse (“cheese”) + Hobel (“(carpenter's) plane”). Calque of Norwegian Bokmål ostehøvel.

noun:Kasuar.tx: From Malay kasuari, probably via Dutch.

adj:knochig.tx: From Knoche, a now-obsolete byform of Knochen, + -ig.

noun:Kyanit.tx: From Ancient Greek κύανος (kúanos, “blue”) + -it (used to form names of minerals).

noun:Konter.tx: From the verb kontern, from English to counter (originally in the context of boxing). The noun is probably not derived directly from the verb but as a clipping of the noun Konterschlag (“counterstrike, backlash”), from kontern + Schlag. Compare also the prefix konter-, from French contre, which influenced the phonetic form of these words.

noun:Konteradmiral.tx: From konter- + Admiral; calque of French contre-amiral.

noun:Kommodore.tx: Borrowed from English commodore. Doublet of Kommandeur.

noun:Klüngel.tx: From Late Middle High German klüngel, klungel, from earlier klüngelīn, klungelīn, from Old High German clungelīn, a diminutive form of clunga (“ball”), ultimately from the root of Kolben (“piston”).

noun:Kien.tx: From Middle High German kien, from Old High German kien, from Proto-West Germanic *kēn.

noun:Kattun.tx: Borrowed from Dutch katoen, ultimately from Arabic قُطُن (quṭun).

noun:Konsultation.tx: Learned borrowing from Latin cōnsultātio, since the 16th century.

noun:Korso.tx: From Italian corso in the archaic sense of “horse race” (for which now corsa), since such celebrations were originally (and still sometimes are) performed with coaches. Doublet of Kurs.

verb:krempeln.tx: Variant of krempen, from Krempe (“brim of a hat”).

noun:Kanin.tx: From Middle Low German kanīn, konīn, probably through Middle Dutch connijn from Old French connin, northern variant of connil, from Latin cunīculus. Compare English cony.

verb:knattern.tx: Since the late 17th century, probably from Central German dialects. Ultimately of imitative origin. Perhaps comparable to knittern (“to crease, crumple”), with which it shares an ablaut relationship.

noun:Kaffer.tx: Borrowed from English kaffir, from Arabic كافر. Doublet of Kafir.

verb:knüllen.tx: From Middle High German knüllen, from Old High German knullen, from Proto-Germanic *knuzlijaną (“to bump, to knock, to mash”), ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *gen- (“to squeeze, to pinch”). Cognate with English knell and Swedish knulla (“to fuck, to have sex”).

noun:Kelter.tx: From Middle High German kelter, kalter, from Old High German calcture, from Latin calcātūra.

verb:keltern.tx: Middle High German keltern, compare Kelter (“press”).

noun:Kebab.tx: From Arabic كَباب (kabāb), partly through Turkish kebap. Further origin uncertain.

noun:Kumpan.tx: From Middle High German kompān, kumpān, from Old French compain (“friend; companion”), from Late Latin compāniō (literally “he with whom one shares one's bread”), from com- + pānis (with + bread).

noun:Kommiss.tx: 16th century, originally in the sense “provisions, anything distributed to the troops”. The modern sense likely by backformation from compounds such as Kommissbrot, Kommissrock etc. Further probably from Latin commissum (“that which is entrusted, committed”).

noun:Kamikaze.tx: Borrowed from Japanese 神風 (kamikaze, “divine wind”).

verb:kleckern.tx: Iterative with -ern of earlier klecken (“to spill, splatter”) (see also Klecks).

verb:knebeln.tx: 17th century, derived from Knebel, from Middle High German knebel, from Old High German knebil. The word originally meant a stick used to tighten a tie or to bind something to, later also the tie itself. Dutch knevelen shows the same semantic development, being used chiefly for “to gag”, but also in the broader sense “to tie up”.

noun:Karbonade.tx: Borrowed from French carbonnade, itself borrowed from Italian carbonata or Occitan carbonada, both ultimately from Latin carbō (“charcoal; coal”).

noun:Korporal.tx: 17th century, borrowed from French corporal, an alteration (after corps) of Middle French caporal, from Italian caporale.

intj:kusch.tx: Originally hunting jargon, from French couche! (“lie down!”), from coucher. The use for “shoo” may or may not be the same word, see ksch for more.

noun:Konkordat.tx: From Medieval Latin concordatum, from Latin concordāre (“to agree”).

noun:Klapsmühle.tx: Klaps + Mühle, originally WWI military slang.

noun:Klampfe.tx: Upper German, from Middle High German klimpfen, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *klampō, related to Proto-West Germanic *klammjan. Cognate with English clamp.

noun:Kringel.tx: From Middle High German kringel, diminutive of krinc, from Old High German *kring, from Proto-Germanic *kringaz, whence Dutch kring. Chiefly a Central German, i.e. northern, word, reinforced by Middle Low German kringel.

noun:Kalesche.tx: From a West Slavic language, perhaps Czech kolesa or Polish kolasa. Compare French calèche.

noun:Kopfkissenbezug.tx: Kopfkissen + Bezug. While Bezug being from ziehen (<< Proto-Germanic *teuhaną < Proto-Indo-European *dewk-), compare typologically powłoczka, на́волочка (návoločka) (<~ волочи́ть (voločítʹ)). Also compare Norwegian Nynorsk putetrekk, dynetrekk (<<+ *trakjaną < *trekaną).

verb:kielholen.tx: Borrowed from Low German kilhalen, adapted to German holen. Compare Dutch kielhalen.

noun:Kapuziner.tx: Calque of Italian cappuccino; equivalent to Kapuze + -iner.

noun:Krösus.tx: Borrowed from Latin Croesus, from Ancient Greek Κροῖσος (Kroîsos).

noun:Kniekehle.tx: From Middle High German kniekel; equivalent to Knie (“knee”) + Kehle (“throat, pit”).

noun:Karacho.tx: Early 20th century, from Spanish carajo (literally “penis”), which is used as a vulgar intensifier. At first attested in the sense “gallop, maximum speed of a rider”, hence probably a humorous substitution for dated Karriere (“gallop, career”).

noun:Kreuzotter.tx: Kreuz (“cross”) + Otter (“adder”), from the cross-shaped markings on its back.

noun:Krieche.tx: From Middle High German krieche, from Old High German *kriehha (attested in kriehboum). Cognate with Middle Dutch crieke (modern kriek), Middle Low German krêke (modern Kreke, Kreike). Further origin uncertain, but predominantly believed to be from Proto-West Germanic *Krēkō (“Greek”). The fruit in question may have been spread along the Danube, but “Greek” might also have been used simply in the …

phrase:koste es, was es wolle.tx: Literally, “it may cost what it will”. Probably after French coûte que coûte. Compare the variant above, which is equivalent to the French variant quoi qu'il (en) coûte, further the early attestation below (in a translation from French), and finally Dutch koste wat kost, which last is clearly a loan translation.

noun:Knüttel.tx: From Middle High German knüttel, from Old High German chnutil, ultimately from the root of Knoten (“knot”).

noun:Kindermord.tx: From Kind + -er- + Mord. Cognate with Dutch kindermoord.

noun:Käsekästchen.tx: From Käse (“cheese”) + Kästchen (“box, case”), probably an alteration of a pleonastic *Kastkästchen or *Caissekästchen (in the latter form with French caisse).

noun:Kantate.tx: From Cantata (first attested in 1712), from Italian cantata (1638), from Medieval Latin cantata (1314), perfect passive participle of Latin canto (“to sing”)

noun:Knaster.tx: Borrowed from Dutch knaster, from Spanish canasto (“basket”).

noun:Käseglocke.tx: From Käse (“cheese”) + Glocke (“bell”), after its bell-like shape.

verb:kneipen.tx: From Middle Low German knîpen, which entered Central German dialects of Late Middle High German and natively underwent the diphthongisation into kneipen. See kneifen for the further development.

verb:knoten.tx: From Middle High German knoten. Equivalent to Knoten + -en.

noun:Konvertit.tx: Borrowed from obsolete English convertite, from French convertir, from Latin converto.

noun:Kohldampf.tx: From Rotwelsch, first attested in 1835 as Kolldampf. Tautological compound of Kohler, Koller (“hunger”) + Dampf (“hunger”, literally “steam”). Not related to Russian голод (golod, “hunger”), German Kohl (“cabbage”).

noun:Kemenate.tx: From Old High German kemināta, from Late Latin camināta, feminine of caminātus (“having a fireplace”), from camīnus (“fireplace”); see also Polish komnata. Cognate with English chimney.

noun:Kommerz.tx: Borrowed from French commerce, from Latin commercium.

noun:Kurschatten.tx: From Kur (“cure, stay at a health resort”) + Schatten (“shadow; someone who follows or escorts another continuously”). Health resorts are considered fertile ground for affairs because people usually go there unaccompanied (besides other possible factors).

noun:Kreol.tx: English creole/Creole or French créole, from Portuguese crioulo.

noun:Klimmzug.tx: From klimmen (“to climb”) + Zug (“a pull, move”).

noun:Kolophonium.tx: From Early New High German Colofonie, from Latin (resina) Colophōnia, from Ancient Greek Κολοφών (Kolophṓn), an ancient city in Ionia.

noun:Klunte.tx: From a German Low German dialect, likely related to Middle Low German *klōt, from Old Saxon *klōt, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *klautaz or *klūtaz (“ball”). Doublet of Kloß and Klöten.

noun:Katheder.tx: 16th century, from Latin cathedra, from Ancient Greek καθέδρα (kathédra).

noun:Kriegshetzer.tx: Krieg + -s- + Hetzer, attested since the 2nd half of the 19th century.

verb:knobeln.tx: Allied to a widely diffused dialectic form knöbel (Upper German), knöwel (Middle German and Low German), ‘joint,’ especially of the fingers.

noun:Konfekt.tx: Middle High German confect, Medieval Latin cōnfectum.

noun:Klitsche.tx: 19th century, from East Central German dialects. Further origin uncertain. Plausibly from Polish kleć (“outhouse”), from Proto-Slavic *klětь. Alternatively from klitschen (“to splat, slap”), a variant of klatschen.

noun:Kustos.tx: Borrowed from Latin custōs. Compare (obsolete) English custos (literally “warden”).

noun:Kreator.tx: Borrowed from Latin creātor, equivalent to kreieren + -ator. Doublet of Kreateur.

noun:Kaldaunen.tx: Borrowed from Medieval Latin caldūna. Compare Old French chaudun, source of English chawdron.

noun:Knebelvertrag.tx: From knebeln (“to gag”) + Vertrag (“contract”). Compare Dutch wurgcontract (literally “strangling contract”).

noun:Karaffe.tx: Borrowed from French carafe or Italian caraffa.

noun:Kimono.tx: Borrowed from Japanese 着(き)物(もの) (kimono, “clothing”).

noun:Klistier.tx: Borrowed from Late Latin clysterium, from Latin clyster, from Ancient Greek κλυστήρ (klustḗr).

verb:kerben.tx: From Middle High German kërben, from Old High German kërban, from Proto-West Germanic *kerban (“to carve, cut”).

noun:Käs.tx: Borrowed from Alemannic German Käs. Austrian German variant of Käse (“cheese”) (alongside Kas which is mainly used outside of Vorarlberg). Used in compounds referring to certain dishes that contain cheese such as Käsknöpfle.

noun:Kas.tx: Borrowed from Bavarian Kas. Austrian German variant of Käse (“cheese”) (alongside Käs which is mainly used in Vorarlberg). Mainly used in compounds referring to certain dishes that contain cheese such as Kasnocken, Kaspressknödel and Erdäpfelkas.

verb:koitieren.tx: Denominalization of Koitus, a learned borrowing from Latin coitus.

noun:Korpsgeist.tx: Calque of French esprit de corps

noun:Krüger.tx: Krug (“pub; bar”) + -er (“-er”) or Low German Kröger (“innkeeper”)

noun:Knorren.tx: Inherited from Middle High German knorre.

noun:Kastell.tx: From Middle High German kástel (“fortified castle, city”), from Old High German kastel, and its doublet Middle High German kastḗl (“castle”), from Middle Dutch casteel, from Picardian Old French castel. Both ultimately from Latin castellum, which also directly influenced the modern form and sense.

noun:Kieker.tx: German Low German Kieker, Middle Low German kiker, by surface analysis, kieken + -er.

intj:Kek.tx: Probably from English kek or its origin. See there for more.

noun:Kek.tx: May be derived from Etymology 1. Has also been claimed to derive from Turkish kek.

noun:Krampe.tx: Standardized since the 17th century. From Central and Low German dialects, from northern Middle High German and Middle Low German krampe f, from Old High German crampo, Old Saxon krampo m, from Proto-West Germanic *krampō, from Proto-Germanic *krampô. Cognate with southern Old High German crampho. Remarkably, modern descendants of the latter, such as Bavarian Krampen m (“bent prong, pickaxe”), …

verb:krankfeiern.tx: Univerbation of krank (“sick, ill”) + feiern (“to celebrate”).

noun:Kontrollfreak.tx: Calque of English control freak, Kontrolle + Freak.

noun:Kolchose.tx: Backformed from the plural of Kolchos, from Russian колхо́з (kolxóz), contraction of коллекти́вное хозя́йство (kollektívnoje xozjájstvo, “collective farm, household”).

noun:Krähwinkel.tx: Coined by German dramatist and writer August von Kotzebue in 1802, from the play Die deutschen Kleinstädter. By surface analysis, Krähe (“crow”) + Winkel (“corner”).

noun:Kinderkreuzzug.tx: Kind + -er- + Kreuzzug, calque of Latin peregrīnātiō puerōrum.

verb:kollaborieren.tx: From French collaborer + -ieren, from Latin collabōrō.

verb:koalieren.tx: Shortened from earlier koalisieren, from French coaliser.

phrase:kommste heut nicht, kommste morge.tx: Literally, “if you don't come today, you'll come tomorrow”. Some sources trace it back to Colognian küss de hück nit, küss de morje, but the saying is attested in various dialect dictionaries. (Colognians are by stereotype easygoing and workshy, which may be the reason for the association.) Compare also Dutch kom ik er vandaag niet, dan kom ik er morgen.

verb:kraxeln.tx: 18th century, at first in the form krachzeln. Further origin uncertain. Either from Bavarian krageln (“to bend one’s legs”) or denominal from Kraxe (“basket borne on the back”) + -eln.

verb:kungeln.tx: From Kunkel (“distaff”) + -en, from the (private) conversations while spinning yarn in groups.

noun:Kriegsfuß.tx: Krieg + -s- + Fuß, calque of French (sur le) pied de guerre.

verb:konferieren.tx: Borrowed from French conférer. Distantly, a near–piecewise doublet of gebären, but with the French infinitive verbal ending -er added as German -ieren.

verb:kalben.tx: From Middle High German kalben. By surface analysis, Kalb + -en.

noun:Knilch.tx: Ca. 1900, of uncertain origin. The two main theories are: * From the adjective knollig (“bulbous”, archaically “ruff, boorish”). Also attested with umlaut as knöllicht. * From Central Franconian Knünich (“canon, kind of clergyman”, figuratively “withdrawn, somber person”), from Old High German canunih (12th c.), from Latin canonicus. A form with /l/ appears to be unattested in the dialects, but …

noun:Köm.tx: From Low German Köm (“caraway”), contracted (as [køːm] < [køːmm̩] < [køːmn̩]) from older Kömen, from Middle Low German kȫmen, from Proto-West Germanic *kumīn, from Latin cuminum, from Ancient Greek κύμινον (kúminon). Doublet of Kümmel.

noun:Kanoniker.tx: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin canonicus + -er, from Ancient Greek κανονικός (kanonikós).

noun:Karzer.tx: Borrowed from Latin carcer (“prison”). Doublet of Kerker (“dungeon”).

verb:kodifizieren.tx: From Kodex with suffix -fizieren, from Latin cōdex.

noun:Kombinat.tx: Calque of Russian комбинат (kombinat), using Latin combīnātum, the substantivized neuter singular of combīnātus (perfect passive participle of combinō). By surface analysis, kombinieren + -at.

noun:Krypta.tx: Borrowed from Latin crypta, from Ancient Greek κρυπτή (kruptḗ), female form of the adjective κρυπτός (kruptós).

noun:Kack.tx: Byform of Kacke. An onomatopoeic creation relating to the sound a baby makes when pressing while defecating (“a-a-”); compare Aa machen as well as Latin cacō, Ancient Greek κακκάω (kakkáō).

noun:Kasperl.tx: Diminutive of the name Kaspar, via Biblical Hebrew גִּזְבָּר (gizbar) from Classical Syriac ܓܙܒܪܐ (gēzaḇrā), from Old Persian *ganzabarah, from Old Median *ganǰabarah. By surface analysis, Kaspar + -erl.

noun:Kandelaber.tx: 18th century, borrowed from French candélabre, from Latin candelabrum.

noun:Kinkerlitzchen.tx: Kinkerlitz m + -chen, from French quincaille(rie) (“metal hardware”) + -chen (diminutive suffix), originally in reference to worthless jewellery.

noun:Komtur.tx: Middle High German kumtur, from Old French commendeor, from Medieval Latin commendātor.

verb:klacken.tx: From klack (interjection) + -en. First attested in the 17th century.

verb:kiebitzen.tx: From older kiewischen, kiebitschen, meaning “to search, strip-search, investigate” in thieves’ cant (Rotwelsch). Further origin uncertain. Possibly from Yiddish כובש זײַן (koyvesh zayn, “to oppress, distress”), from Hebrew כבש (kāvāš). Later associated with Kiebitz (“lapwing”), but direct derivation from it is unlikely.

noun:Kilch.tx: From Alemannic German Kilch, from Middle High German kelch, from Old High German chelch. Doublet of Kelch "double chin".

noun:Kombiwagen.tx: From Kombinationskraftwagen, often further shortened to just Kombi.

noun:Kontrolletti.tx: From the 1974 song "Jonny Controletti" by German musician Udo Lindenberg, seemingly formed from Kontrolle or kontrollieren and the Italian suffix -etti, meant to resemble Italian surnames like Moretti or Marchetti.

noun:Kuckuckskind.tx: From Kuckuck (“cuckoo”) + -s- + Kind (“child”). After the cuckoo’s habit of leaving its eggs in other birds’ nests.

intj:ksch.tx: Probably imitative, compare Russian кыш (kyš). Alternatively from kusch (command for a dog to lie down). The form kusch also appears in the sense of “shoo”, but this might be through secondary confluence.

noun:Kahm.tx: From Middle High German kan, from Vulgar Latin cana, from Latin cānus (“gray”).

noun:Kleinvieh.tx: From klein (“small”) + Vieh (“livestock”). Compare Dutch kleinvee, French menu bétail, African English smallstock.

noun:Koprozessor.tx: Borrowed from English coprocessor. By surface analysis, ko- + Prozessor.

noun:Katzentisch.tx: From Katze (“cat”) + -n- + Tisch (“table”), the place where cats eat, originally referring to the floor the table is placed on.

noun:Kloppe.tx: Deverbal from kloppen (“to hit, beat up”).

noun:Kufiya.tx: Borrowed from Arabic كُوفِيَّة (kūfiyya), in accordance with the German DMG transcription, while the form Keffije represents the vulgar transcription of the earlier 20th century, and Keffiye probably follows English keffiyeh, keffiye.

noun:Kaffeefahrt.tx: From Kaffee (“coffee”) + Fahrt (“trip”), from coffee and cake usually being served at these events.

noun:Keyboarder.tx: From Keyboard + -er or directly from English keyboarder.

noun:Kendo.tx: Borrowed from Japanese 剣道(けんどう) (kendō)。

verb:karden.tx: From late Middle High German karten. By surface analysis, Karde + -en.

noun:Kreosot.tx: Coined by German natural philosopher Carl Reichenbach in 1832, from Ancient Greek κρέας (kréas, “flesh”) + σωτήρ (sōtḗr, “preserver”) for its use as an antiseptic and meat preservative.

phrase:Kinder, die was wollen, kriegen w.tx: Literally, “children who want something get something on their thighs / buttocks”. Probably a calque from Low German. The anatomical use of Bollen is especially Westphalian, where the phrase is attested in 1912 as Kinner, die wat wollen, kriegt wat op den Bollen (note that wollen is preterite in this case). Otherwise it is also found in Low German with a rhyme on Bille (cf. Dutch bil), e.g. …

noun:Käfigkampf.tx: Compound of Käfig + Kampf; calque of English cage fight

noun:Kumpe.tx: From Kumpan + -e, with retraction of the accent to the first syllable.
